Abaddon.who: Abaddon, the angel of the bottomless pit and 'destroyer' named in Revelation 9:11, later counted among the orders of devils.

Abbas Joachimus.who: Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), Calabrian abbot whose apocalyptic prophecies of a coming age of the Spirit were widely cited.

Abbey.who: Battle Abbey, Sussex, built on the site of the Battle of Hastings (1066).

Abdalonymus.who: Abdalonymus, poor gardener of royal descent whom Alexander the Great made king of Sidon, as told by Quintus Curtius.

Abdera.who: Abdera, Greek city on the coast of Thrace, home of Democritus; its people were proverbial for stupidity.

Abderites.who: The Abderites, citizens of Abdera in Thrace, who in the pseudo-Hippocratic letters sent for Hippocrates to cure Democritus of supposed madness.

Abderum.who: Abderus, favourite of Hercules in Greek myth, killed by the man-eating mares of Diomedes; Abdera was said to be named after him.

Abel.who: Abel, son of Adam, murdered by his brother Cain (Genesis 4); also named in the title of Ambrose's treatise De Cain et Abel.

Abigail.who: Abigail, wife of the churlish Nabal, who placated David and later married him (1 Samuel 25).

Abraham.basis: second passage is the cant term 'Abraham men'
Abraham.who: Abraham, the Hebrew patriarch, husband of Sarah; 'Abraham men' (second passage) were vagrant beggars who feigned madness.

Abraham Avenezra.who: Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–c. 1164), Spanish Jewish biblical commentator, astrologer and scholar.

Abraham Ortelius.who: Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), Antwerp cartographer, compiler of the atlas Theatrum Orbis Terrarum.

Abrocomas.basis: possibly Habrocomes of Xenophon of Ephesus, but the 'Epist. 21' reference is unclear

Absalom.who: Absalom, son of King David, who rebelled against his father and was killed; David mourned him (2 Samuel 13–18).

Absyrtus.who: Apsyrtus, brother of Medea in Greek myth, whom she killed and dismembered to delay their father Aeetes' pursuit of the Argonauts.

Abulensis.who: Alfonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), 'Abulensis', bishop of Ávila, Spanish theologian and voluminous biblical commentator.

Abydos.who: Abydos, ancient Greek city on the Asian shore of the Hellespont (Dardanelles).

Abyssines.who: The Abyssinians, people of the Christian empire of Ethiopia, whose ruler Europeans identified with Prester John.

Academic.basis: applied to Carneades, head of the New Academy
Academic.who: A member of the Academy, the Platonic school, which under Carneades (2nd century BC) taught scepticism.

Acarnania.who: Acarnania, region of western Greece on the Ionian Sea, bordering the Ambracian Gulf.

Accius.basis: Persius' 'Accius' is usually taken as Attius Labeo, translator of Homer; second citation unclear

Acco.basis: known from Greek proverb collections and Plutarch
Acco.who: Acco, proverbial foolish old woman of Greek tradition who went mad on seeing her aged face in a mirror; used as a bogey.

Achaia.basis: Burton uses it loosely for Greece
Achaia.who: Achaea, region of the northern Peloponnese, Greece; also the Roman name for the province covering southern Greece.

Achaicis.who: Achaica, Book 7 of Pausanias' Description of Greece, covering Achaea.

Achan.who: Achan, Israelite who stole a Babylonian garment and gold from Jericho, bringing disaster on Israel, and was stoned (Joshua 7).

Achans.who: Achan, Israelite stoned for stealing devoted spoil at Jericho (Joshua 7); used figuratively for church robbers.

Ache.who: Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle), city in western Germany, Charlemagne's residence and burial place.

Achelous.who: Achelous, Greek river god who wrestled Hercules for Deianira and lost a horn.

Achilles.who: Achilles, greatest Greek hero of the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad; his spear both wounded and healed Telephus.

Achitophel.who: Ahithophel, David's counsellor who joined Absalom's revolt and hanged himself when his advice was rejected (2 Samuel 15–17).

Acholzius.basis: likely a garbled form of Scholtzius, whose collected epistles are cited
Acholzius.who: Laurentius Scholzius (1552–1599), Silesian physician of Breslau, who published collections of medical letters and consilia.

Acmet Bassa.who: Gedik Ahmed Pasha (d. 1482), Ottoman grand vizier and general, executed by Sultan Bayezid II.

Acon.who: Acre (Akko), port in present-day northern Israel, besieged and taken by the Third Crusade (1189–1191).

Acontius.who: Acontius, legendary youth of Ceos who won Cydippe by tricking her into an oath written on an apple; told by Callimachus, Ovid (Heroides 20–21) and Aristaenetus.

Acosta.basis: First two passages are on America and the tropics (José de Acosta); 'Em. Acosta' is Emmanuel (Manuel) Acosta
Acosta.who: José de Acosta (1540–1600), Spanish Jesuit, author of the Historia natural y moral de las Indias; the Japan reference is to Manuel da Costa's 1568 Jesuit commentary.

Acroceraunian.who: The Acroceraunian (Ceraunian) mountains, a range ending in a headland on the coast of ancient Epirus, now the Karaburun peninsula in south-west Albania.

Acrocorinthus.who: Acrocorinth, the high rocky citadel above ancient Corinth in Greece.

Actaeon.who: Actaeon, mythical hunter turned into a stag by Diana and torn apart by his own hounds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3).

Acte.who: Claudia Acte, a freedwoman who was the Emperor Nero's mistress, as Tacitus relates in the Annals.

Actium.who: Actium, a promontory and town in Acarnania in western Greece, where Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC.

Actuarius.who: Joannes Zacharias Actuarius (c. 1275–c. 1328), Byzantine court physician who wrote on medicines, urines and the spirits.

Ad Marciam.who: Seneca's Consolatio ad Marciam, a letter of consolation to Marcia on the death of her son.

Adam.who: Adam, the first man in Genesis.

Adamantus.who: Adamantius (4th century AD), Greek sophist and physician whose Physiognomonica paraphrases Polemon's treatise on physiognomy.

Adamians.who: The Adamiani, an early Christian sect described by Epiphanius and Augustine, who worshipped naked in imitation of Adam's innocence.

Adamites.who: The Adamites, a radical sect in early-15th-century Bohemia, linked to the 'Picards', who went naked and were said to hold women in common.

Adelaide.who: Adelaide of Hesse, daughter of Landgrave Henry II of Hesse and wife from 1341 of Casimir III the Great of Poland, who neglected her.

Adelhelmus.who: Aldhelm (c. 639–709), abbot of Malmesbury and later bishop of Sherborne, author of the Latin treatise De virginitate.

Aden.who: Aden, a port on the Gulf of Aden in southern Arabia, now in Yemen.

Admetus.who: Admetus, mythical king of Pherae in Thessaly, whose wife Alcestis agreed to die in his place (Euripides, Alcestis).

Adonided.basis: A garbled form in a list of Near Eastern idols; Burton's note cites Ezek. 8:14 (the weeping for Tammuz, i.e. Adonis)
Adonided.who: Probably Adonis (the Syrian Tammuz), the god mourned by women in Ezekiel 8:14.

Adonijah.who: Adonijah, son of King David, who tried to take the throne before Solomon and was later put to death (1 Kings 1–2).

Adonis.who: Adonis, the beautiful youth loved by Venus and killed by a boar; in one passage it is the flower named after him, the anemone.

Adonis. Petronius.basis: A segmentation error that runs two names together, Adonis and Petronius

Adorni.who: The Adorno, a Genoese family who led a faction against the rival Fregoso family and supplied several doges in the 14th–16th centuries.

Adramelech.who: Adrammelech, a god of the Sepharvites to whom children were burned (2 Kings 17:31).

Adrasteia.who: Adrasteia, Greek goddess of inescapable retribution, identified with Nemesis.

Adrian.basis: Burton names 'the sixth' and 'the fourth' explicitly
Adrian.who: Adrian VI (1459–1523), Dutch pope 1522–23, an austere reformer; the third passage means Adrian IV (Nicholas Breakspear), the English pope of 1154–59.

Adrian Turnebus.who: Adrien Turnèbe (1512–1565), French classical scholar and royal professor at Paris, author of the Adversaria.

Adrianople.who: Adrianople, now Edirne in European Turkey, an Ottoman capital and later a favourite residence of the sultans.

Adricomius.who: Christian van Adrichem (Adrichomius) (1533–1585), Dutch Catholic priest, author of the Theatrum Terrae Sanctae, a description of the Holy Land.

Aeacus.who: Aeacus, mythical king of Aegina who became one of the three judges of the dead, with Minos and Rhadamanthus.

Aeetes.who: Aeetes, mythical king of Colchis and father of Medea, keeper of the Golden Fleece.

Aegean.who: The Aegean Sea, between Greece and Asia Minor.

Aegeria.who: Egeria, the Roman nymph said to have been the consort and counsellor of King Numa Pompilius.

Aegeus.who: Aegeus, legendary king of Athens and father of Theseus, who threw himself into the sea thinking his son was dead.

Aegidius Maserius.who: Gilles Maserius (Aegidius Maserius), early-16th-century French humanist who edited the Argonautica of Valerius Flaccus with a commentary.

Aegina.who: Aegina, Greek island in the Saronic Gulf, within sight of Athens.

Aegisthus.who: Aegisthus, in Greek legend the lover of Clytemnestra, with whom he murdered Agamemnon; the line quoted is from Ovid's Remedia amoris.

Aegle.who: Aegle, a woman mocked in an epigram of Martial (1.72) for her bought false teeth.

Aegyptiacos.who: The Egyptians, here the Egyptian embalmers described by Herodotus.

Aelia Laelia Crispis.who: Aelia Laelia Crispis, the name in the enigmatic Latin inscription at Bologna ('nec vir nec mulier…'), a riddle that many scholars tried to explain.

Aelian Montaltus.who: Filipe (Elijah) Montalto (1567–1616), Portuguese Jewish physician, author of the Archipathologia (1614) on diseases of the head.

Aeliensian.basis: Olympic wrestlers named in Philostratus; the form seems to be a corruption of 'Elean'.
Aeliensian.who: The Eleans, people of Elis in the Peloponnese, where the Olympic games were held.

Aemilia.basis: Dionysius is cited and tells of the Vestal Aemilia; Burton's ordeal detail does not match exactly.
Aemilia.who: Aemilia, legendary Vestal virgin whose innocence was proved by a miracle, as told by Dionysius of Halicarnassus.

Aemilius Probus.who: Aemilius Probus, the name under which Cornelius Nepos's Lives of Famous Commanders (including Epaminondas) circulated in the Renaissance.

Aen Silv.who: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), later Pope Pius II, humanist author of the love story of Euryalus and Lucretia.

Aeneas.who: Aeneas, Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid and lover of Dido; in the first passage 'Aeneas Silv.' is Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini (Pius II).

Aeneids.who: Virgil's Aeneid, epic poem on Aeneas.

Aenobarbi.who: The Ahenobarbi ('bronze-beards'), a branch of the Roman Domitian family, to which Nero belonged by birth.

Aeolian.who: The Aeolian or Lipari Islands, a volcanic group north of Sicily.

Aeolus.who: Aeolus, keeper of the winds, who obeys Juno in Aeneid book 1.

Aeschinus.who: Aeschinus, the young lover in Terence's comedy Adelphoe, adopted son of Micio.

Aesculapius.who: Aesculapius (Asclepius), Graeco-Roman god of healing, with famous temples where the sick sought cures.

Aesop’s Fables.who: The fables ascribed to Aesop, legendary Greek storyteller of the 6th century BC.

Aetolia.who: Aetolia, region of west-central Greece north of the Gulf of Corinth, kingdom of Oeneus in legend.

Afranius.who: Lucius Afranius (fl. c. 100 BC), Roman writer of comedies on Roman themes (fabulae togatae), known only from fragments.

Africani. Chinae.who: The Africans (as described by Leo Africanus); 'Chinae' starts the next phrase, 'China root', a medicinal root.

Africanus.who: Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder (236–183 BC), conqueror of Hannibal, praised in verses by Ennius.

Africk.who: Africa; in the first passage the Roman province that Sallust governed under Caesar.

Agaberta.basis: legendary northern witch cited from Boissard; cannot trace his source with confidence

Agamemnon.who: Agamemnon, king of Mycenae and Greek leader at Troy, murdered by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover.

Agamemnon’s Iphigenia.who: Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon, whom he sacrificed at Aulis to get winds for the Greek fleet.

Aganella.basis: Athenaeus credits ball play to Nausicaa on Agallis's authority; Burton's name and story look like a corruption of this.
Aganella.who: Agallis of Corcyra, woman grammarian who, as Athenaeus records, credited Nausicaa with inventing ball games; Burton garbles the account.

Agapetianus.basis: the advice to rulers on using God's gifts fits Agapetus's Exposition; the Latinised form is unusual.
Agapetianus.who: Agapetus the Deacon (6th century), Constantinople cleric whose book of advice to Emperor Justinian taught rulers humility and gratitude to God.

Agasicles.who: Agasicles, Eurypontid king of Sparta (6th century BC), father of King Ariston.

Agasthenes.who: Agasthenes, minor character in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Agathinus.who: Claudius Agathinus (1st century AD), Greek physician of the Pneumatic school, known for writing on cold bathing.

Agathoclea.who: Agathoclea (d. c. 203 BC), mistress of Ptolemy IV Philopator of Egypt; she and her mother Oenanthe had great power at court.

Agathocles.who: Agathocles (361–289 BC), tyrant and later king of Syracuse, who was said to be a potter's son.

Agathon.who: Agathon (c. 448–c. 400 BC), Athenian tragic poet, whose victory banquet is the setting of Plato's Symposium; an epigram ascribed to Plato is addressed to him.

Agathonem.who: Agathon (c. 448–c. 400 BC), Athenian tragic poet and Plato's favourite, host of the Symposium.

Agave.who: Agave, in Greek myth daughter of Cadmus and mother of Pentheus, whom she tore apart in a Bacchic frenzy.

Agent.who: The 'agent' (active) intellect, as opposed to the 'patient' (passive) intellect, in scholastic psychology.

Aggregator.who: Jacopo de' Dondi (1298–1359), Paduan physician, called 'the Aggregator' from his compilation of remedies, the Aggregator medicamentorum.

Agincourt.who: Agincourt (Azincourt), village in northern France where Henry V defeated the French in 1415.

Agis.basis: The Timaea story is about Agis II; Plutarch tells the small-wife story of his father Archidamus II, so Burton may have mixed them up in the first passage.
Agis.who: Agis II (d. c. 400 BC), king of Sparta, whose wife Timaea was seduced by the exiled Alcibiades.

Agnus Castus.who: Agnus castus, the chaste tree (Vitex agnus-castus), a medicinal plant.

Agrigentum.who: Agrigentum (Greek Akragas), ancient Greek city on the south coast of Sicily, now Agrigento.

Agrip.basis: Burton often cites Agrippa's De vanitate for satire on learned self-conceit, and this abbreviation is how he cites him.
Agrip.who: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), German humanist and occultist, author of De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum, an attack on human learning.

Agrippina.basis: Tacitus' 'nescia tolerandi' describes the grieving elder Agrippina; the Claudius passage fits the younger.
Agrippina.who: In Tacitus, Agrippina the Elder (d. AD 33), widow of Germanicus; elsewhere Agrippina the Younger (AD 15–59), wife of Claudius and rival of Lollia Paulina and Calpurnia.

Aguilonius.who: François d'Aguilon (1567–1617), Flemish Jesuit mathematician, author of Opticorum libri sex (1613).

Agur.who: Agur son of Jakeh, the otherwise unknown sage to whom Proverbs 30 is ascribed.

Ahasuerus.who: Ahasuerus, the Persian king of the Book of Esther, usually identified with Xerxes I (r. 486–465 BC).

Aix.who: Aix-la-Chapelle (Latin Aquisgranum), now Aachen in western Germany, known for its hot springs.

Ajax.who: Ajax son of Telamon, Greek hero at Troy, who went mad and killed himself when Achilles' arms were awarded to Ulysses.

Alabanda.who: Alabanda, ancient city of Caria in south-western Asia Minor, near modern Çine, Turkey.

Alanus.who: Alain Chartier (c. 1385–c. 1430), French poet and royal secretary, whom Margaret of Scotland, wife of the future Louis XI, is said to have kissed.

Alardus.basis: Burton names him next to Marbodeus in a list of writers on gems.
Alardus.who: Alardus of Amsterdam (Alaard van Amstel, 1491–1544), Dutch humanist who edited Marbod's poem on precious stones.

Albania.who: Albania, the Balkan region on the Adriatic, then under Ottoman rule.

Albanian.who: Albania here means ancient Caucasian Albania, west of the Caspian; its king sent Alexander a huge dog that disdained to fight lesser beasts (Pliny 8.149).

Albans.who: St Albans, Hertfordshire, beside the site of Roman Verulamium.

Albategnius.who: al-Battani (Albategnius, c. 858–929), Arab astronomer of Raqqa, whose astronomical tables corrected Ptolemy.

Albertinus.basis: Possibly Francesco Albertini, Jesuit theologian, but not certain.

Albertinus Bottonus.who: Albertino Bottoni (d. 1596), physician and professor of medicine at Padua.

Albertus.who: Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), Dominican philosopher, theologian and natural scientist; books of 'secrets' and marvels also circulated under his name.

Albertus Durer.who: Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), German painter and engraver of Melencolia I (1514), who also wrote on human proportion.

Albubater.who: Abu Bakr al-Hasan ibn al-Khasib (Albubater), 9th-century Persian astrologer, author of a much-printed Latin treatise on nativities.

Albumazar.who: Abu Ma'shar (Albumazar, 787–886), Persian astrologer of Baghdad, known for his theory that great conjunctions of planets govern the rise and fall of empires.

Alcander.basis: The marginal note cites the Epistles of Phalaris.
Alcander.who: Alcander, a man to whom one of the spurious Letters of Phalaris is addressed.

Alcestis.who: Alcestis, in Greek myth wife of King Admetus of Pherae, who agreed to die in his place.

Alcibiades.who: Alcibiades (c. 450–404 BC), Athenian statesman and general, Socrates' companion, notorious for his luxury and ostracised by Athens.

Alcinous.who: In the first passage, Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians in the Odyssey; in the others, Alcinous (2nd century AD), Middle Platonist author of the Didaskalikos.

Alcmena.who: Alcmena, in Greek myth wife of Amphitryon and mother of Heracles by Zeus, praised in the Hesiodic Shield of Heracles.

Alcoran.who: The Qur'an ('Alcoran'), the Muslim scripture, known to Burton through Latin translations.

Aleacman.who: The Haliacmon, a river of Macedonia in northern Greece (modern Aliakmonas), said by Pliny to whiten the cattle that drink from it.

Alecto.who: Alecto, one of the three Furies (Erinyes) of Greek and Roman myth.

Alegabalus.who: Elagabalus (Heliogabalus), Roman emperor 218–222, notorious for luxury and debauchery; 'Alegabalus' is a variant form of the name.

Aleppo.who: Aleppo, the great trading city of northern Syria.

Alexander.who: In the medical passages, Alexander of Tralles (c. 525–c. 605), Byzantine physician; in the second passage, Alexander the Great (356–323 BC).

Alexander Achilles.who: Alessandro Achillini (1463–1512), Bolognese philosopher, physician and anatomist.

Alexander Albertinus à Rocha.basis: Latin form and exorcism context match Albertini's Malleus daemonum (1620)
Alexander Albertinus à Rocha.who: Alessandro Albertini of Rocca, early seventeenth-century Italian Catholic writer on exorcism, author of a *Malleus daemonum*.

Alexander Aphrodiseus.who: Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. c. 200 AD), Aristotelian commentator; a book of *Problems* went under his name.

Alexander Aphrodisiensis.who: Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. c. 200 AD), Aristotelian commentator; a book of *Problems* went under his name.

Alexander Benedictus.who: Alessandro Benedetti (c. 1450–1512), Italian physician and anatomist who taught at Padua.

Alexander Massaria.who: Alessandro Massaria (1510–1598), Italian physician and professor of medicine at Padua.

Alexander Medices.who: Alessandro de' Medici (1510–1537), first duke of Florence, murdered by his kinsman Lorenzino.

Alexander Munificus.who: Alexander of Lincoln (d. 1148), bishop of Lincoln, called 'the Magnificent', who built castles including Newark.

Alexander Pheraeus.who: Alexander of Pherae, tyrant of Thessaly (r. c. 369–358 BC), murdered by his wife Thebe.

Alexander Piccolomineus.who: Alessandro Piccolomini (1508–1579), Sienese scholar who wrote a treatise on the relative size of earth and water.

Alexander Severus.who: Severus Alexander, Roman emperor 222–235, whose life is in the *Historia Augusta* under Lampridius' name.

Alexander Trallianus.who: Alexander of Tralles (c. 525–c. 605), Byzantine Greek physician and medical writer.

Alexander ab.who: Alessandro Alessandri (1461–1523), Neapolitan jurist and antiquary, author of the *Genialium dierum libri sex*.

Alexander ab Alexandro.who: Alessandro Alessandri (1461–1523), Neapolitan jurist and antiquary, author of the *Genialium dierum libri sex*.

Alexanders.who: Alexander the Great (356–323 BC), used here as the type of a great conqueror.

Alexandretta.who: Alexandretta (Scanderoon), the port now called İskenderun in southern Turkey.

Alexandria.who: Alexandria, the port city of Egypt.

Alexandrinus.who: Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215), Christian theologian, author of the *Stromata*.

Alexandrum Benedictum.who: Alessandro Benedetti (c. 1450–1512), Italian physician and anatomist who taught at Padua.

Alexis.who: First, 'Alexis of Piedmont', supposed author of a popular book of secrets; second, Alexis (c. 375–275 BC), Greek comic poet; third, the beloved boy of Virgil's second Eclogue.

Alfakins.who: Alfaquís (Arabic al-faqīh), Muslim doctors of law who act as judges.

Alfraganus.who: Al-Farghani (Alfraganus, 9th century), Arab astronomer whose summary of Ptolemaic astronomy was widely read in Latin.

Alfredus.basis: marginal citation of a law on remarriage; Alfred is the usual lawgiver cited under this Latin form
Alfredus.who: Alfred the Great (849–899), king of Wessex, cited as a lawgiver.

Alhazen.who: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, c. 965–c. 1040), Arab mathematician and astronomer, author of the great treatise on optics.

Aliacensis.who: Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), French cardinal and theologian who wrote on astronomy and astrology.

Alkermes.who: Alkermes, a cordial confection coloured with kermes (the scarlet insect dye).

Alkindus.who: Al-Kindi (c. 801–c. 873), Arab philosopher, mathematician and writer on medicine, including the doses of compound medicines.

Alkmaar.who: Alkmaar, a town in North Holland, the Netherlands.

Alli.who: Ali ibn Abi Talib (d. 661), Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law and the fourth caliph, revered by the Shia.

Allobroges.who: The Allobroges, a Gallic people between the Rhône and the Isère, in modern Savoy and Dauphiné.

Allon Bakuth.who: Allon-bachuth ('oak of weeping'), the oak below Bethel where Deborah was buried (Genesis 35:8).

Almagest.who: The *Almagest*, Ptolemy's great treatise on astronomy (2nd century AD).

Almutens.who: Almutens: in astrology, the planets with the most dignities in a given house or degree of a horoscope.

Aloes.who: Aloes, a bitter purgative drug made from aloe juice.

Aloysius Cadamustus.who: Alvise Cadamosto (c. 1432–1483), Venetian explorer who sailed to West Africa in Portuguese service.

Alpheratius.basis: Writer said to be printed twenty-four times in Spanish; I can't settle who is meant.

Alpheus.who: Alpheus, the god of the river Alpheus in the Peloponnese, who in myth chased the nymph Arethusa under the sea to Syracuse.

Alphonsine.who: The Alfonsine Tables, astronomical tables made in the 1270s under Alfonso X of Castile and based on the Ptolemaic system.

Alphonsus.basis: Different kings: the second passage means the astronomer Alfonso X of Castile; the third is a king of Aragon and Sicily (Alfonso V); the first is a king imitated by his courtiers.

Alphonsus Junior.who: Alfonso II of Naples (1448–1495), Duke of Calabria and later King of Naples, whose tutor and secretary was the humanist Giovanni Pontano.

Alphonsus de Castro.who: Alfonso de Castro (1495–1558), Spanish Franciscan theologian and author of Adversus omnes haereses (1534).

Alpine.who: Of the Alps; the 'Alpine mice' that sleep all winter are marmots.

Alps.who: The Alps, the mountain range of central Europe.

Alsarius Crucius.who: Vincenzo Alsario della Croce (1576–1634), Genoese physician and author of De quaesitis per epistolam in arte medica centuriae.

Alsatia.who: Alsace, the region on the upper Rhine, then part of the Holy Roman Empire and now in France.

Alterative.who: Alteratives: medicines that change or correct the body's state, as opposed to purgatives.

Altmuhl.who: The Altmühl, a river in Bavaria that flows into the Danube; Charlemagne's canal (Fossa Carolina) was meant to join it to the Rezat/Rednitz.

Altopilus.basis: Marginal source citation only; I can't identify it.

Altrix.who: Latin term for the nutritive faculty of the vegetal soul.

Amadis de Gaul.who: Amadis de Gaula, Spanish chivalric romance put into its standard form by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo (printed 1508), widely translated and imitated.

Amanuenses.who: Secretaries or scribes who write from dictation.

Amaranthus.basis: The philosopher arguing about Epicurus and Democritus with friends matches the setting of Prodromos's dialogue.
Amaranthus.who: Amarantus, the old philosopher of Theodore Prodromos's twelfth-century Byzantine dialogue 'Amarantus, or the Loves of an Old Man'.

Amaryllis.who: Amaryllis, a stock name for a beloved shepherdess in pastoral poetry, from Theocritus and Virgil.

Amasis.who: Amasis II, Egyptian pharaoh (r. 570–526 BC), who according to Herodotus made every Egyptian declare his means of living each year.

Amatorio Dialogo.who: Plutarch's Amatorius (Dialogue on Love), one of the Moralia.

Amatus Lusitanus.who: Amatus Lusitanus (João Rodrigues de Castelo Branco, 1511–1568), Portuguese Jewish physician and author of the Curationum medicinalium centuriae.

Amazons.who: The Amazons, legendary female warriors; here those said by explorers to live in South America.

Ambergris.who: Ambergris, a substance from the sperm whale, used as a cordial.

Ambition.who: Ambition, a passion, used here as a heading.

Ambracia.who: Ambracia, an ancient city on the Ambracian Gulf in north-western Greece, at the site of modern Arta.

Ambrosian.basis: Passages 1 and 3 mean the Ambrosian College (Ambrosiana) in Milan, founded by Federico Borromeo; passage 2 means 'ambrosial', like ambrosia.

Ambrosius.who: Ambrose of Alexandria (d. c. 250), wealthy patron of Origen, who paid for the stenographers and copyists who took down his works.

America. Paulus Jovius.basis: Form mis-cut; the name is Paulus Jovius.
America. Paulus Jovius.who: Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), Italian historian and bishop of Nocera, author of a Descriptio Britanniae.

Americans.who: The native peoples of America, especially the Mexicans.

Americus Vesputius.who: Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512), Florentine navigator and explorer of the New World, after whom America is named.

Amestris.who: Amestris, wife of the Persian king Xerxes I; Herodotus (book 9) tells of her revenge on the wife of Masistes.

Amington.who: Amington, a village by the river Anker near Tamworth, then in Warwickshire and now in Staffordshire.

Ammonites.who: The Ammonites, an ancient people east of the Jordan who appear in the Old Testament.

Ammonius.basis: The second passage clearly means Zacharias's opponent; the first may instead mean Ammonius Saccas.
Ammonius.who: Ammonius, son of Hermias (c. 440–c. 520), Neoplatonist teacher at Alexandria, attacked in Zacharias of Mytilene's dialogue 'Ammonius'.

Amnon.who: Amnon, eldest son of King David, who raped his half-sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13).

Amoreos.who: Medieval medical term (amor hereos) for love-sickness as a disease, used by Gerardus de Solo.

Amosis.basis: Mela 1.9 reckons 330 kings and over 13,000 years before Amasis; Burton's form follows that passage.
Amosis.who: Amasis II (r. 570–526 BC), Saite pharaoh of Egypt; Mela counts the long line of Egyptian kings before him.

Ampelis.who: Ampelis, an older courtesan who advises the younger Chrysis about lovers in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Amphiaraus.who: Amphiaraus, Argive seer and hero of the Seven against Thebes; his oracle of healing dreams was at Oropus on the border of Attica.

Amphion.who: Amphion, son of Zeus and Antiope, whose lyre playing made the stones move into place to build the walls of Thebes.

Amphitheatro Boterus.basis: Boterus is Botero; 'Amphitheatro' seems to be a garbled marginal citation of the work.
Amphitheatro Boterus.who: Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617), Piedmontese political writer, author of the Relazioni universali, a survey of the world's states.

Amphitrite.who: Amphitrite, Greek sea goddess, a Nereid and the wife of Poseidon (Neptune).

Amphitryon.who: Amphitryon, Theban husband of Alcmena; Jupiter took on his form to father Hercules on her, as in Plautus's comedy Amphitruo.

Amsterdam.who: Amsterdam, chief city of Holland and a refuge for English separatist congregations.

Amsterdamian.who: Of Amsterdam: the English separatist congregations (Brownists and others) that went into exile there.

Amurath.who: Murad II (1404–1451), Ottoman sultan, who broke through and destroyed the Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth in 1446.

Amy.who: A conventional mistress's name in a fickle lover's list; not a historical person.

Amymone.who: Amymone, one of the Danaids, who was loved by Poseidon (Neptune) at Argos.

Amynander.who: Amynander, the fictional friend to whom one of Aristaenetus's Love Letters is addressed.

Amyntas.basis: Different bearers in the two passages.
Amyntas.who: First, Amyntas, the lamenting lover-shepherd of pastoral verse; second, Amyntas I of Macedon, father of King Alexander I (r. c. 498–454 BC).

Anabaptist.who: Anabaptists, radical Protestants of the Reformation who rejected infant baptism.

Anabaptists.who: Anabaptists, radical Protestants of the Reformation who rejected infant baptism, and many of whom refused to bear arms.

Anacharsis.who: Anacharsis (fl. 6th century BC), Scythian prince who visited Athens and was counted a sage, known for his sharp sayings.

Anacreon.who: Anacreon (c. 570–c. 485 BC), Greek lyric poet of wine and love who lived at the court of Polycrates of Samos.

Anacreon Bathyllum.who: Anacreon (c. 570–c. 485 BC), Greek lyric poet, with the boy Bathyllus, whom he loved and celebrated in his poems.

Anacreons.who: Poets like Anacreon (c. 570–c. 485 BC), the Greek lyric poet of love and wine.

Anagrams.who: Word puzzles made by rearranging letters.

Anakims.who: The Anakim, a race of giants in Canaan according to the Old Testament (Numbers 13, Deuteronomy 2).

Anatillo.basis: Pizarro's title is usually given as marqués de los Atabillos; Burton's form appears to be a corruption of it.
Anatillo.who: Atavillos (Atabillos), a district in Peru; Francisco Pizarro was made Marquess of it.

Anatomist.who: Someone who studies the structure of the body by dissection.

Anaxagoras.who: Anaxagoras of Clazomenae (c. 500–428 BC), Greek natural philosopher who worked in Athens and held that the heavenly bodies were made of earthy matter.

Anaxarchus.who: Anaxarchus of Abdera (fl. 4th century BC), philosopher of the school of Democritus and companion of Alexander the Great.

Anaximenes.who: Anaximenes of Miletus (fl. 6th century BC), Ionian natural philosopher.

Anchises.who: Anchises, Trojan prince whom Venus loved and by whom she bore Aeneas.

Ancile.who: The ancile, the sacred shield said to have fallen from heaven in the reign of Numa and kept by the Salian priests in Rome.

Ancona.who: Ancona, Adriatic port in central Italy; its March was part of the Papal States.

Ancyra.basis: Ancyra usually means this city, but its link to an Apollo oracle is uncertain; Burton may mean another place.
Ancyra.who: Ancyra, city of Galatia in Asia Minor, now Ankara, Turkey.

Andalusia.who: Andalusia, the southern region of Spain.

Andes.who: The Andes, the mountain chain of western South America.

Andreas Baccius.who: Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), Italian physician to Pope Sixtus V and author of De naturali vinorum historia, a treatise on wines.

Andreas Tiraquellus.who: André Tiraqueau (1488–1558), French jurist who wrote a learned commentary on Alexander ab Alexandro's Genialium dierum.

Andreas Victorellus.basis: The Latin form and the subject of guardian angels fit Vittorelli; I am not certain of his dates.
Andreas Victorellus.who: Andrea Vittorelli, Italian priest of Bassano and author of a treatise on guardian angels (early 17th century).

Andrew.who: St Andrew the Apostle, patron saint of Scotland.

Andrew Boorde.who: Andrew Boorde (c.1490–1549), English physician and former Carthusian, author of the *Dyetary of Helth* and the *Breviary of Helthe*.

Andrew Gallus.basis: A physician of Trent cited through Mattioli; I cannot identify him further.

Androcles.who: Androcles, a character in the pseudo-Lucianic dialogue *Charidemus*: the uncle of the handsome youth Cleonymus, who gives the feast.

Andromache.who: Andromache, Hector's wife in Homer's Iliad. After the fall of Troy she was made the captive and concubine of Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, who had killed Hector.

Andromeda.who: Andromeda, the Ethiopian princess of Greek myth whom Perseus rescued from a sea-monster; Persina in Heliodorus's *Aethiopica* is her descendant.

Andronicus.basis: He is listed among tyrants destroyed by their own subjects, which fits him best of the several Andronici.
Andronicus.who: Andronikos I Komnenos (r. 1183–1185), Byzantine emperor and tyrant, deposed and torn to pieces by the people of Constantinople.

Anemone.who: The anemone, the flower said to have sprung from the blood of Adonis.

Angelica.who: Angelica, the heroine of Boiardo's *Orlando innamorato* and Ariosto's *Orlando furioso*; Orlando's love for her drives him mad.

Angelo.who: Henri de Joyeuse, duc de Joyeuse (1563–1608), French nobleman and marshal who became a Capuchin friar under the name Frère Ange (Father Angelo).

Angelus Politianus.who: Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), Florentine humanist, poet and classical scholar of the Medici circle.

Angelus Salas.who: Angelo Sala (1576–1637), Italian physician and chemist, author of *Anatomia antimonii* (Anatomy of Antimony).

Angerianus Erotopaedium.who: The *Erotopaegnion*, a collection of Latin love poems by the Neapolitan humanist poet Girolamo Angeriano (c.1470–1535).

Angerianus Erotopaegnion.who: The *Erotopaegnion*, a collection of Latin love poems by the Neapolitan humanist poet Girolamo Angeriano (c.1470–1535).

Angerona.who: Angerona, an obscure Roman goddess linked with silence and with anguish (angor); her festival, the Divalia, fell in December.

Angerona Dea.who: Angerona, an obscure Roman goddess linked with silence and with anguish (angor); her festival, the Divalia, fell in December.

Anian.who: The Strait of Anián, a legendary strait between Asia and America that was supposed to offer a north-west passage to China.

Anjou.who: Anjou, a French duchy on the Loire. Its duke Henry was elected King of Poland in 1573 and later became Henry III of France.

Anker.who: The River Anker, which flows through north Warwickshire past Nuneaton and Atherstone to join the Tame at Tamworth.

Anna Perenna.who: Anna Perenna, a Roman goddess of the circling year, whose riotous festival was held on 15 March.

Annals.who: The *Annales ecclesiastici* (1588–1607) of Cardinal Cesare Baronius, a massive year-by-year history of the Church.

Anno Dom.basis: Latin 'in the year of the Lord'.

Antenor.who: Antenor, a wise Trojan elder in Homer's Iliad; in Plato's *Symposium* Alcibiades pairs him with Nestor as a counterpart to Pericles.

Anteros.who: Anteros, the Greek god of returned love, brother of Eros and son of Aphrodite.

Antevorta.who: Antevorta, a Roman goddess (or aspect of Carmenta) who looks forward to the future; paired with Postvorta, who looks back to the past.

Anthony.who: Different bearers: St Anthony of Egypt (c.251–356), desert hermit; Antony in Cornwall, Richard Carew's seat; Francis Anthony (1550–1623), London physician who promoted aurum potabile.

Anthony Brunus.basis: Cited as a writer on the immortality of the soul; I cannot identify him with certainty.

Anthony Foscarinus.who: Paolo Antonio Foscarini (c.1565–1616), Neapolitan Carmelite theologian whose 1615 letter argued that Copernican earth-motion agrees with Scripture.

Anthony Guevara.who: Antonio de Guevara (c.1481–1545), Spanish Franciscan bishop and court writer, author of the *Reloj de príncipes* (Dial of Princes) and the *Epístolas familiares*.

Anthony Lodovicus.basis: The Latin form, Burton's note 'Olysipponensis medicus' (physician of Lisbon) and the title *De pudore* all fit him.
Anthony Lodovicus.who: Antonio Luís (Antonius Ludovicus), sixteenth-century Portuguese physician of Lisbon, author of *De pudore*.

Anthony Musa.who: Antonius Musa (fl. 23 BC), physician to the emperor Augustus. A treatise on betony, *De herba vettonica*, was ascribed to him.

Anthony Perez.who: Antonio Pérez (1540–1611), secretary of state to Philip II of Spain, who fled into exile and wrote political *Aphorisms* and letters.

Anthony Rusca.who: Antonio Rusca, priest and doctor of the Ambrosian College in Milan, author of *De inferno et statu daemonum* (1621).

Anthony Schets.basis: The Schetz family of Grobbendonk held the command at 's-Hertogenbosch (Sylvaducis) in this period; Burton's account of the combat is loose.
Anthony Schets.who: Anthonie Schetz, baron of Grobbendonk, commander at 's-Hertogenbosch, whose men fought Bréauté's troop in the celebrated combat of February 1600.

Anthony Verdeur.basis: Anglicised form of Du Verdier; the anecdote fits his miscellany of curious stories
Anthony Verdeur.who: Antoine du Verdier (1544–1600), French bibliographer and compiler of the miscellany *Diverses leçons*, a collection of strange stories.

Anthony Zara.who: Antonio Zara, bishop of Pedena (Pićan) in Istria, author of *Anatomia ingeniorum et scientiarum* (1615), a treatise on wits and learning.

Anthony Zara Pap. Episc.who: Antonio Zara, bishop of Pedena (Pićan) in Istria, author of *Anatomia ingeniorum et scientiarum* (1615), which is divided into sections and members.

Anthropophagi.who: The man-eaters or cannibals of ancient and travellers' report.

Anti-Aristarchus.who: *Ant-Aristarchus* (1631), by the Louvain professor Libert Froidmont (Fromondus), attacking Lansbergen's defence of the Copernican system.

Antichrist.who: The Antichrist of Christian prophecy, whom Protestant polemic identified with the papacy.

Antichrists.who: Opponents of Christ and false teachers, in the sense of 1 John 2:18.

Anticyrae.who: Anticyra, the name of ancient towns in Phocis and near Malis in Greece, famous for hellebore and visited as a cure for madness.

Anticyrian.who: A native of Anticyra in Greece, the town famous for hellebore and its use as a cure for madness.

Antigonus.basis: Antigonus Gonatas (letter to Zeno), Antigonus I Monophthalmus (Alexander's successor), and the father of a Demetrius are different men

Antimony.who: The metal antimony, used in early modern chemical medicine as an emetic and purge.

Antinoe.who: Antinoöpolis, a city in Middle Egypt founded by Hadrian in AD 130 in memory of Antinous.

Antinous.who: Antinous (d. AD 130), the Bithynian youth loved by the emperor Hadrian, who deified him after he drowned in the Nile.

Antioch.who: Antioch on the Orontes, capital of Seleucid and Roman Syria; now Antakya in Turkey.

Antiochian.who: Of Antioch; here Lucian of Antioch (d. 312), priest, biblical scholar and martyr.

Antiochian Daphne.who: Daphne, the famous grove and pleasure resort with Apollo's temple near Antioch; now Harbiye in Turkey.

Antiochus.basis: Antiochus IV Epiphanes in 1 Maccabees, and Antiochus I, son of Seleucus, in the Stratonice story

Antiochus Epiphanes.who: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (c. 215–164 BC), Seleucid king of Syria, known for his eccentric behaviour.

Antiope.who: Antiope, the Amazon queen whom Theseus carried off in Greek legend.

Antipater.who: Antipater of Tarsus (2nd century BC), Stoic philosopher; Stobaeus preserves extracts from his writings on marriage.

Antiphanes.who: Antiphanes (4th century BC), prolific Athenian poet of Middle Comedy, known now from fragments.

Antipheron.who: Antipheron of Oreus, mentioned by Aristotle (*De memoria*) as a man who took his mental images for real things.

Antiphila.basis: A stock name for a beloved, paired with Dulcinea; Terence's heroine is the best-known bearer
Antiphila.who: Antiphila, the beloved girl in Terence's comedy *Heauton Timorumenos*; Burton uses the name for any lover's mistress.

Antipodes.who: The people who live on the opposite side of the globe, or that region itself.

Antitycho.who: *Antitycho* (1621), by Scipione Chiaramonti of Cesena, attacking Tycho Brahe's view that comets are celestial and that the heavens are fluid.

Antoninus.basis: Different emperors called Antoninus: a scholarly emperor, the Baths of Antoninus (Caracalla), and a model of worth (probably Pius)

Antoninus Caracalla.who: Caracalla (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, 188–217), Roman emperor, said to have lusted after his stepmother Julia Domna.

Antoninus Verus.who: Lucius Verus (130–169), co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius and husband of Lucilla, who was rumoured to have poisoned him.

Antonius.basis: Mark Antony in the first two passages; Dr Francis Anthony, the London maker of aurum potabile, in the third

Antonius Musa.who: Antonius Musa (1st century BC), physician to Augustus; a treatise on the herb betony is ascribed to him.

Antony.who: Mark Antony (83–30 BC), Roman triumvir and lover of Cleopatra, who killed himself after his defeat.

Antony Diogenes.who: Antonius Diogenes, Greek novelist of the Roman imperial period, author of *The Wonders beyond Thule*, known from Photius' summary.

Antonys.who: Hermits like St Antony of Egypt (c. 251–356), the founder of Christian monasticism.

Antwerp.who: Antwerp, the port and printing centre in Brabant, now in Belgium.

Anubis.who: Anubis, the jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead, worshipped alongside Isis.

Anytus.who: Anytus (d. after 399 BC), Athenian democratic politician and chief accuser of Socrates; Plutarch makes him Alcibiades' lover.

Aomar.who: Umar ibn al-Khattab (c. 584–644), the second caliph after Muhammad.

Aonius Palearius.who: Aonio Paleario (c. 1500–1570), Italian humanist, author of the Latin poem *De animorum immortalitate*; he was executed for heresy.

Apelles.basis: Passages 2–3 mean the painter. Passage 1 means 'Apelles', the pen-name of the Jesuit astronomer Christoph Scheiner, who wrote on sunspots.
Apelles.who: Apelles (4th century BC), the most celebrated painter of ancient Greece, court painter to Alexander the Great.

Apennine.who: The Apennines, the mountain chain running down the length of Italy.

Apician.who: Adjective from Marcus Gavius Apicius (1st century AD), the proverbial Roman gourmet of Tiberius's reign.

Apicius.who: Marcus Gavius Apicius (1st century AD), a Roman gourmet under Tiberius who, according to Seneca, poisoned himself when his fortune had shrunk.

Apiciuses.who: Plural of Apicius, the proverbial Roman gourmet of Tiberius's reign; here, extravagant gluttons in general.

Apis.who: Apis, the sacred bull worshipped at Memphis in ancient Egypt.

Apocalypse.who: The Apocalypse, or Book of Revelation, the last book of the New Testament.

Apollo.basis: In passage 3, 'Apollo' is the costly dining room of Lucullus described by Plutarch, not the god himself.
Apollo.who: Apollo, Greek god of prophecy, music and healing, whose oracle was at Delphi.

Apollo Alexicacus.who: Apollo under the title Alexikakos, 'averter of evil', worshipped at Athens as the god who turned away plague.

Apollo Pythius.who: Pythian Apollo, the god as he was worshipped at Delphi, the seat of his oracle.

Apollodorus.basis: Several different men. Passage 1: Apollodorus of Phalerum, a disciple of Socrates. Passage 3: Apollodorus, tyrant of Cassandreia, in Plutarch. Passage 2: unclear.

Apollonia.who: St Apollonia of Alexandria (d. c. 249), virgin martyr whose teeth were broken out; invoked against toothache.

Apollonides Cous.who: Apollonides of Cos (5th century BC), Greek physician at the Persian court who, according to Ctesias, seduced a royal princess and was buried alive.

Apollonius.basis: Each passage cites Philostratus's Life or refers to his feats; Burton's 'scholar of Socrates' is a slip.
Apollonius.who: Apollonius of Tyana (1st century AD), Neopythagorean sage and wonder-worker, whose Life was written by Philostratus.

Apollonius Tyanaeus.who: Apollonius of Tyana (1st century AD), Neopythagorean sage and wonder-worker; Hierocles set him against Christ, and Eusebius answered Hierocles.

Apollonius Tyaneus.who: Apollonius of Tyana (1st century AD), Neopythagorean sage reputed a magician, whose Life was written by Philostratus.

Apollonius’ Conics.who: The Conics of Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BC), the classic Greek treatise on conic sections.

Apolog.who: The Apologia (De magia) of Apuleius, his defence against the charge of winning the widow Pudentilla by magic.

Apona.who: Aponus, the hot springs near Padua; modern Abano Terme.

Aponensis.who: Pietro d'Abano (Petrus de Abano, c. 1257–c. 1316), physician, philosopher and astrologer of Padua.

Apostate.who: Julian the Apostate (331–363), Roman emperor who renounced Christianity, and a friend of the philosopher Maximus of Ephesus.

Apostle.who: St Paul the Apostle, author of the Epistle to the Galatians.

Appian.who: The Appian Way (Via Appia), the Roman road from Rome to Brundisium.

Appius Claudius.basis: Passage 1: Appius Claudius the decemvir, overthrown in 449 BC. Passage 2: Appius Claudius Caecus, the blind censor of 312 BC.

Apries.who: Apries (Wahibre, reigned 589–570 BC), pharaoh of Egypt's 26th dynasty, whose pride and fall Herodotus describes.

Apuleius Apol.who: The Apologia (De magia) of Apuleius (2nd century AD), his courtroom defence against a charge of magic.

Apulia.who: Apulia (Puglia), the region of south-eastern Italy.

Aquaria.basis: It is named among Italian baths in Trincavelli's consilia; the name fits Acquaria in the Frignano district.
Aquaria.who: Probably Acquaria, a spa with mineral springs in the Apennines near Modena, in northern Italy.

Aquitaine.who: Aquitaine, the region of south-western France.

Aquitaines.who: The people of Aquitaine in south-western France, the countrymen of Salvian.

Aquitania.who: Aquitaine (Latin Aquitania), the region of south-western France.

Arabia.who: Arabia, the peninsula of south-western Asia, including the Arabian Desert (Arabia Deserta).

Arabia Deserta.who: Arabia Deserta, the ancient name for the desert interior of northern Arabia, between Syria and Mesopotamia.

Arabia Petraea.who: Arabia Petraea, the ancient name for north-western Arabia, from Sinai to modern Jordan; later the Roman province of Arabia.

Arabian.who: Of Arabia or the Arabs, used here of Arabic-writing scholars and physicians.

Arabian Phoenix.who: The phoenix, a fabulous bird said to live in Arabia and to be reborn from its own ashes.

Arabians.who: The Arabs, here chiefly the Arabic-writing philosophers and physicians of the Middle Ages.

Arachne.who: Arachne, the Lydian weaver in Ovid's Metamorphoses who challenged Athena (Minerva) to a contest and was turned into a spider.

Aragon.who: Aragon, a kingdom in north-eastern Spain whose kings also ruled Sicily and Naples.

Arar.who: The Arar, the Latin name of the Saône, a river in eastern France that flows into the Rhône at Lyon.

Araspas.who: Araspas, the Median nobleman in Xenophon's Cyropaedia who was given charge of the captive Panthea and fell in love with her.

Arbatel.basis: Burton knew the Celestina, and the name is paired with Terence's Antiphila, another literary mistress.
Arbatel.who: Areusa, a courtesan in Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, used here as a typical mistress's name.

Arcades.who: The Arcadians, the people of Arcadia in the central Peloponnese.

Arcadia.basis: The third passage refers to the book's authors, not the region.
Arcadia.who: Arcadia, the mountainous region of the central Peloponnese in Greece; in the third passage, Sir Philip Sidney's prose romance Arcadia.

Arcadian.who: Of Arcadia, the region of the central Peloponnese.

Arcadius.who: Arcadius (c. 377–408), Roman emperor in the East from 395, son of Theodosius I; he ruled alongside his brother Honorius in the West.

Archelaus.who: Archelaus I, king of Macedon (reigned c. 413–399 BC), who invited poets including Euripides to his court.

Archidamus.basis: Augustine's De sermone Domini in monte I.16 tells this story of Acindynus; Burton's name and emperor look garbled.
Archidamus.who: Probably Septimius Acindynus, praetorian prefect and consul in 340, named in Augustine's story of the wife at Antioch who gave herself to save her husband.

Archilochus.who: Archilochus of Paros (7th century BC), Greek lyric and iambic poet, proverbial for bitter satire.

Archimedes.who: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), Greek mathematician and inventor.

Archippe.who: Archippe, an Athenian courtesan whom Athenaeus's Deipnosophistae (book 13) names as the mistress of the aged Sophocles.

Archytas Tarentinus.who: Archytas of Tarentum (fl. 4th century BC), Pythagorean philosopher, mathematician and statesman, friend of Plato.

Arcite.who: Arcite, the Theban knight in Chaucer's Knight's Tale who competes with Palamon for Emily and dies after winning her.

Arctic.who: The Arctic Circle, the parallel that bounds the north polar region.

Ardelions.who: Ardelio (from Latin), a busybody or meddler; Burton glosses the word himself.

Ardes.who: Ardres, a town in the Pas-de-Calais, northern France, near the site of the Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520).

Arethusa.who: Arethusa, a nymph pursued by the river-god Alpheus; she became a spring on Ortygia at Syracuse (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5).

Aretine’s Lucretia.basis: Burton's note cites Barth's Latin translation of an Italian original; Lucretia is the speaker's name in that version.
Aretine’s Lucretia.who: Lucretia, the courtesan who speaks in a dialogue derived from Pietro Aretino's Ragionamenti, in Caspar Barth's Latin version, the Pornodidascalus.

Aretius.who: Benedictus Aretius (Benedikt Marti, c. 1522–1574), Swiss Reformed theologian and naturalist at Bern.

Areusa.basis: Burton knew the Celestina, and the name is paired with Terence's Antiphila, another literary mistress.
Areusa.who: Areusa, a courtesan in Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, used here as a typical mistress's name.

Argenis.who: Argenis, the heroine of John Barclay's Latin political romance Argenis (1621), loved by Poliarchus.

Argentocoxus.who: Argentocoxus, a Caledonian chief in the time of Septimius Severus's British campaigns; Cassius Dio records his wife's retort to the empress Julia Domna.

Argonauts.who: The Argonauts, the heroes who sailed with Jason in the Argo to fetch the Golden Fleece; here, figuratively, explorers.

Argos.who: Argos, an ancient Greek city in the Argolid, north-eastern Peloponnese.

Argus.who: Argus, the hundred-eyed giant set by Juno to guard Io; Mercury lulled him to sleep with his pipe and killed him.

Ariadne.who: Ariadne, the Cretan princess who helped Theseus, was abandoned by him on Naxos (Dia), and was then wedded by Dionysus.

Arian.who: Arius (c. 256–336), Alexandrian priest whose teaching that the Son was created gave rise to Arianism; he was a rival of Bishop Alexander.

Arians.who: Arians, followers of Arius's doctrine that denied the Son was co-eternal with the Father; in Burton's day, applied to Polish and Transylvanian antitrinitarians.

Arias Montanus.who: Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), Spanish biblical scholar and orientalist, editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.

Arica.who: Arica, a Pacific port then in Spanish Peru, now in northernmost Chile.

Aries.who: Aries, the Ram, first sign of the zodiac, whose first point marks the spring equinox.

Arion.who: Arion of Methymna (fl. c. 600 BC), legendary Greek lyre-player and poet, said to have been carried ashore by a dolphin charmed by his music.

Ariostos.who: Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), Italian poet of the chivalric romance Orlando furioso; Burton's plural means poets like him.

Aristagoras.who: Aristagoras, public secretary of Cyzicus during Mithridates' siege (73 BC), to whom Persephone appeared in a dream, according to Plutarch's Life of Lucullus.

Aristarchus.basis: first passage is the grammarian, second the Samian astronomer
Aristarchus.who: Two different men: Aristarchus of Samothrace (c. 216–144 BC), Alexandrian grammarian and Homeric critic; and Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BC), astronomer who held that the earth moves.

Aristarchus Samius.who: Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–c. 230 BC), Greek astronomer who proposed that the earth turns and orbits the sun.

Aristides.who: Aristides 'the Just' (c. 530–c. 468 BC), Athenian statesman and general, ostracised in 482 BC and later recalled.

Aristides Milesius.who: Aristides of Miletus (fl. c. 100 BC), Greek author of the Milesian Tales, erotic stories that Plutarch says were found in Crassus' baggage.

Aristippus.who: In the first two passages, Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435–c. 356 BC), pleasure-seeking pupil of Socrates; in the third, a guest at a feast in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Aristo Ephesius.basis: the Parallela minora tells this story of Aristonymus of Ephesus; Burton's 'Aristo' looks like a shortened form of the name
Aristo Ephesius.who: Aristonymus of Ephesus, in a tale in the pseudo-Plutarchan Parallela minora: a woman-hater who coupled with a she-ass.

Aristoclea.who: Aristoclea, daughter of Theophanes, heroine of one of Plutarch's Love Stories (Amatoriae narrationes): she died when her suitors Strato and Callisthenes fought over her.

Aristocracies.who: Government by the best citizens; an ordinary noun.

Ariston.who: Ariston, Eurypontid king of Sparta (6th century BC), son of Agasicles, who took his friend's beautiful wife, according to Herodotus (6.61–63).

Aristonica.basis: the passage names Plutarch's dialogue; I cannot give further details of her with confidence
Aristonica.who: Aristonica, a female musician named in Plutarch's Amatorius among the women who held sway over Hellenistic kings.

Aristophanes.who: Aristophanes (c. 446–c. 386 BC), Athenian comic playwright who mocked Socrates in the Clouds and wrote the Plutus.

Aristophanes’ Plutus.who: Plutus (Wealth, 388 BC), Aristophanes' comedy, in which Poverty argues that she is necessary to mankind.

Aristophanis Ranis.who: Aristophanes' comedy The Frogs (405 BC), given here in its Latin title.

Aristotles.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher; Burton's plural means learned men like him.

Aristotle’s Problems.who: The Problemata, a collection of questions in natural science attributed to Aristotle but largely written by later Peripatetics.

Aristoxenus.who: Aristoxenus of Tarentum (b. c. 375 BC), Peripatetic philosopher and music theorist who held that the soul is a harmony.

Arithmetic.who: The mathematical art of reckoning; an ordinary noun.

Ariulphus.who: Ariulf (d. c. 602), Lombard duke of Spoleto; Paul the Deacon says St Sabinus fought for him at Camerino.

Arius.who: Arius (c. 250–336), Alexandrian priest whose teaching founded Arianism; he died suddenly, reportedly with his bowels bursting.

Arles.who: Arles, a city on the Rhône in Provence, southern France.

Arlette.who: Herleva (Arlette) of Falaise (d. c. 1050), mistress of Robert I, Duke of Normandy, and mother of William the Conqueror.

Armachanus.who: Richard FitzRalph (c. 1300–1360), Archbishop of Armagh ('Armachanus'), a fierce critic of the mendicant friars.

Armena.basis: Xenophon does not seem to name her; 'Armena' appears to be Burton's label for her as 'the Armenian woman'
Armena.who: The wife of Tigranes, son of the Armenian king, in Xenophon's Cyropaedia (Book 3).

Armenian.who: Of Armenia, the kingdom in the Caucasus region; here the Armenian king Tiridates.

Armenians.who: The Armenian Christians of the Armenian Apostolic Church, separate from both the Greek and Roman churches.

Armenus.who: Lapis Armenus, the 'Armenian stone' (a blue copper mineral, probably azurite), used in early modern medicine as a purge for melancholy.

Arminians.who: Followers of the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), who rejected strict Calvinist predestination in favour of universal grace.

Arnaldum.who: Arnau de Vilanova (Arnaldus de Villanova, c. 1240–1311), Catalan physician, author of a treatise on lovesickness (De amore heroico).

Arnaldus.who: Arnau de Vilanova (Arnaldus de Villanova, c. 1240–1311), Catalan physician, author of the Breviarium practicae and medical aphorisms.

Arnaldus Villanovanus.who: Arnau de Vilanova (c. 1240–1311), Catalan physician, author of the Breviarium practicae, the De amore heroico and a regimen of health.

Arnaudus.basis: a Latin poet cited for one verse; cannot be settled

Arnauldus.basis: the anti-Jesuit statistic in French livres fits Arnauld's famous plea
Arnauldus.who: Antoine Arnauld (1560–1619), French advocate whose 1594 pleading for the University of Paris attacked the Jesuits and their wealth.

Arnisaeus.who: Henning Arnisaeus (c. 1575–1636), German physician and Aristotelian political philosopher.

Arnobius.who: Arnobius of Sicca (d. c. 330), North African rhetorician and Christian apologist, author of Adversus nationes.

Arnold.basis: the same 200,000-livre charge is attributed to 'Arnauldus' elsewhere in Burton
Arnold.who: Antoine Arnauld (1560–1619), French advocate whose 1594 pleading against the Jesuits charged them with amassing great wealth.

Arnoldus Tillius.basis: Burton reverses the roles in the case
Arnoldus Tillius.who: Arnaud du Tilh (d. 1560), the impostor who posed as Martin Guerre, tried before the Parlement of Toulouse and executed.

Arnulphus.who: Arnulf of Lisieux (d. 1184), bishop of Lisieux in Normandy, letter-writer and author of Latin epigrams.

Arpinas.who: Latin for 'a man of Arpinum', the hill town southeast of Rome (modern Arpino) where Cicero was born to a family outside the Roman nobility.

Arras.who: Arras, chief town of Artois in northern France, famous for its tapestry hangings.

Arria.who: Arria the Elder (d. AD 42), wife of Caecina Paetus; she stabbed herself first to show him how to die, saying 'Paete, non dolet'.

Arrian.who: Arrian (Flavius Arrianus, c. 86–after 146), Greek historian from Nicomedia, author of the Anabasis of Alexander.

Arruntius.basis: Several Arruntii appear in Tacitus and Seneca, and the passage does not settle which one is meant.

Artaxerxes.basis: Cyrus's battle points to Artaxerxes II; in Ctesias, Apollonides of Cos seduced Amytis, sister of Artaxerxes I.
Artaxerxes.who: In Plutarch's Life: Artaxerxes II Mnemon, Persian king (r. 404–358 BC). In the Apollonides story (from Ctesias), Artaxerxes I's household is meant (r. 465–424 BC).

Artemidorus.basis: Paired with Cardan and Sambucus as dream-interpreters; the grammarian comes from a separate anecdote.
Artemidorus.who: In the dream passages, Artemidorus of Daldis (2nd century AD), author of the Oneirocritica on interpreting dreams; the grammarian frightened by a crocodile is a different man.

Artemisia.who: Artemisia II of Caria (d. c. 350 BC), sister and widow of Mausolus; she built the Mausoleum and was said to have drunk his ashes.

Artephius.who: Artephius, medieval writer on alchemy and magic, probably 12th century, to whom works such as the Clavis majoris sapientiae are attributed.

Arthington.who: Henry Arthington, who in 1591, with Edmund Coppinger, proclaimed William Hacket as Christ in London; he later recanted.

Arthur.who: King Arthur, legendary British king of the Round Table, counted among the Nine Worthies.

Artois.who: Artois, a province in northern France whose capital is Arras.

Asa.who: Asa, king of Judah (c. 913–873 BC), who in his illness 'sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians' (2 Chronicles 16:12).

Ascham.who: Roger Ascham (1515–1568), English humanist and tutor to Elizabeth I, author of Toxophilus (1545), in praise of archery.

Asclepiadean.basis: In Galen's account Thessalus attacked Hippocrates and the ancients, which fits the Asclepiads.
Asclepiadean.who: The Asclepiads, the old Greek medical guild claiming descent from Asclepius, to which Hippocrates belonged; the Methodist Thessalus attacked their teaching.

Asclepiades.basis: The physician is clear in passages 2–3; the 'Grecian' writer on angels in passage 1, cited from Cicogna, is uncertain.
Asclepiades.who: In the medical passages, Asclepiades of Bithynia (fl. c. 100 BC), Greek physician at Rome who rejected humoral theory and treated the frantic with music.

Asclepius.who: The Asclepius, a Hermetic dialogue in Latin attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, which describes making gods dwell in statues.

Asia Minor.who: Asia Minor, the Anatolian peninsula (modern Turkey).

Asianos.who: Latin for 'Asians', the peoples of Asia.

Asiniae.who: Ashima, the god made by the men of Hamath who were resettled in Samaria (2 Kings 17:30).

Asinius Pollio.who: Gaius Asinius Pollio (76 BC–AD 4), Roman statesman and historian, who would not answer Octavian's verses: 'it is not easy to write against one who can proscribe'.

Asmodaeus.who: Asmodeus, the demon of the Book of Tobit, ranked in demonologies as a prince of devils.

Assisi.who: Assisi, a town in Umbria, central Italy, birthplace of St Francis.

Assyria.who: Assyria, used loosely by Burton, as by ancient writers, for Syria and the lands of the Euphrates.

Assyrians.who: The Assyrians, the ancient Mesopotamian empire whose envoy Rabshakeh threatened Jerusalem (2 Kings 18).

Astartes.who: Astarte (biblical Ashtoreth), Phoenician goddess worshipped at Sidon.

Asteroth.who: Ashtaroth (Astarte), the Canaanite and Phoenician goddess whose worship by Israel's neighbours the Old Testament condemns.

Astolpho.who: Astolfo, the English duke in Ariosto's *Orlando Furioso* (1516–32), whose enchanted horn drove everyone who heard it mad with terror.

Astrakhan.who: Astrakhan, city near the mouth of the Volga on the Caspian Sea, in southern Russia.

Astrophel’s Stella.who: Stella, the lady of Sir Philip Sidney's sonnet sequence *Astrophel and Stella* (printed 1591), usually taken to be Penelope Devereux, Lady Rich.

Astyanassa.who: Astyanassa, in Greek legend Helen of Troy's maid, said in the Suda to have been the first to write on sexual positions.

Atalanta.who: Atalanta, the swift-footed huntress of Greek myth who raced her suitors and lost to Hippomenes, who distracted her with golden apples.

Atalantae.who: Atalanta, the huntress of Greek myth; Pliny mentions paintings of her and of Helen at Lanuvium.

Ate.who: Ate, the Greek goddess of folly and ruin, described in Homer as walking softly over men's heads.

Athamas.who: Athamas, mythical king of Orchomenus in Boeotia, driven mad by Juno so that he killed his son Learchus.

Athanasius.who: St Athanasius (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria, author of the *Life of Antony*; other works were also attributed to him.

Athenian Areopagites.who: Members of the Areopagus, the ancient council of Athens that met on the Hill of Ares and held judicial and supervisory powers.

Athenodorus.basis: Pliny does not say which Athenodorus he means; the Philostratus passage plainly concerns another man
Athenodorus.who: In the first passage, the Stoic philosopher Athenodorus of Pliny's ghost story (Letters 7.27), usually taken as Athenodorus Cananites; in the second passage, a different man, a friend named in Philostratus' letters.

Athos.who: Mount Athos, on the easternmost peninsula of Chalcidice in northern Greece; Xerxes cut a canal through its isthmus.

Atlantis.who: Atlantis, Plato's legendary island commonwealth; 'a new Atlantis' alludes to Francis Bacon's utopia *New Atlantis* (1627).

Atlas.who: In the first two passages, Atlas, the Titan who holds up the heavens; in the third, the Atlas Mountains of north-west Africa.

Atlas Geog.basis: the marginal note sits beside the names Mercator and Hondius
Atlas Geog.who: Gerard Mercator's *Atlas* (1595), enlarged and reissued by Jodocus Hondius and his heirs from 1606.

Atlas Geographicus.basis: Burton cites the same work elsewhere as 'Atlas Geog.' next to Mercator and Hondius
Atlas Geographicus.who: Probably the Mercator–Hondius *Atlas*, the standard geographical atlas of Burton's day, with descriptive texts for each region.

Atreus.who: Atreus, mythical king of Mycenae, who took revenge on his brother Thyestes for seducing his wife Aerope.

Attabaliba.who: Atahualpa (c. 1502–1533), the last Inca emperor, who threw down the breviary offered him by Friar Vicente de Valverde at Cajamarca in 1532.

Attalus.who: Attalus II Philadelphus (220–138 BC), brother of Eumenes II of Pergamum; on a false report of Eumenes' death he took the crown and married Queen Stratonice.

Attic.who: Of Attica, the region around Athens; Athenian.

Attica.who: Attica, the region of east-central Greece around Athens.

Atticus.who: Titus Pomponius Atticus (110–32 BC), Roman knight and Cicero's close friend and correspondent; in the first passage 'scurra Atticus' simply means 'Attic buffoon'.

Atwater.basis: Camden's account of the Fossdyke names a Bishop Atwater; William Atwater was the bishop of Lincoln of that name
Atwater.who: William Atwater (d. 1521), bishop of Lincoln from 1514, credited with work on the Fossdyke canal between the Trent and Lincoln.

Aubanus.who: Johann Boemus (Aubanus) (c. 1485–1535), German Hebraist and ethnographer, author of *Omnium gentium mores* (1520), a survey of the customs of nations.

Aubanus Bohemus.who: Johann Boemus (Aubanus) (c. 1485–1535), German humanist from Franconia, author of *Omnium gentium mores* (1520), a survey of the customs of nations.

Auctrix.basis: term for the faculty of growth

Aug.who: Abbreviation for St Augustine of Hippo (354–430), Church Father, whom Burton usually calls 'Austin'.

Augsburg.who: Augsburg, imperial free city in Swabia, southern Germany (now Bavaria).

Augurs.who: The augurs, the Roman college of priests who read the will of the gods from the flight of birds and other signs.

Augusta Livia.who: Livia Drusilla (58 BC–AD 29), wife of the emperor Augustus, called Julia Augusta after his death.

Augustana Pharmacopoeia.who: The Pharmacopoeia Augustana, the official book of medicines of the city of Augsburg, first issued in 1564.

Augustine Friar.who: An Augustinian friar, a member of the order of Augustinian hermits.

Augustine Niphus.who: Agostino Nifo (c.1473–c.1545), Italian Aristotelian philosopher who taught at Padua, Naples and Pisa.

Augustino.who: St Augustine of Canterbury (d. c.604), missionary sent to England by Pope Gregory the Great, whose answers to his questions Bede records.

Aulis.who: Aulis, harbour town in Boeotia on the Euripus strait, where the Greek fleet gathered for Troy.

Aurea Chersonesus.who: The Golden Chersonese of the ancient geographers, generally taken to be the Malay Peninsula.

Aurelian.basis: The footstool story belongs to Valerian, not Aurelian; Burton's name looks like a slip
Aurelian.who: Probably the emperor Valerian (r. 253–260), captured by Shapur I of Persia and said to have been used as his footstool.

Aurelianus.who: In the medical passages, Caelius Aurelianus (5th c.), Latin medical writer on acute and chronic diseases; in the Tiber passage, the emperor Aurelian (r. 270–275).

Aurelius.basis: Listed among emperors who rose from common soldiers; Aurelian fits, Marcus Aurelius does not
Aurelius.who: The emperor Aurelian (r. 270–275), of humble birth, who rose through the army to become emperor.

Aurelius Victor.who: Sextus Aurelius Victor (fl. 4th c.), Roman historian, author of the De Caesaribus, short lives of the emperors.

Aust.who: In the Severn passage, Aust, a village on the Severn estuary in Gloucestershire; in the other, 'Aust.' abbreviates Austin, i.e. St Augustine of Hippo.

Austin. Eusebius.who: Not one name: 'Austin' (St Augustine of Hippo) ends one sentence and Eusebius of Caesarea (c.260–339), church historian, begins the next.

Austria.who: Austria; in the first passage, the House of Austria, i.e. the Habsburg dynasty.

Austrian.basis: The Habsburg lip is well known; the astronomical names were dynastic compliments like the Medicean stars
Austrian.who: Relating to the Habsburgs (House of Austria): the 'Habsburg lip', and 'Austrian stars', new celestial bodies named in compliment to the dynasty.

Autolycus.who: In the first passage, Autolycus, mythical master thief and son of Hermes; elsewhere, Autolycus, the handsome Athenian youth of Xenophon's Symposium.

Avan.who: St Afan, early Welsh saint, to whom the church of Llanafan Fawr near Builth in Breconshire is dedicated.

Ave Marias.who: Hail Marys, the Catholic prayer to the Virgin.

Aventinus.who: Johannes Aventinus (Johann Turmair, 1477–1534), Bavarian humanist historian, author of the Annales Boiorum.

Aventinus Anno.who: Johannes Aventinus (Johann Turmair, 1477–1534), Bavarian historian, author of the Annales Boiorum; 'Anno' belongs to the date that follows.

Avenzoar.who: Avenzoar (Ibn Zuhr, c.1094–1162), Andalusian Arab physician of Seville, author of the Taysir.

Averroes.who: Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), Andalusian philosopher and physician, the great commentator on Aristotle.

Averroist.who: A follower of Averroes, known in Renaissance Italy for denying the immortality of the individual soul.

Averters.who: Medicines that divert the humour, such as clysters; a section heading.

Avignon.who: Avignon, city in Provence, held by the papacy until 1791.

Avoid Satan.who: Christ's rebuke to the tempter (Matthew 4:10), 'Get thee hence, Satan'.

Axiocho.who: The Axiochus, a dialogue on death once ascribed to Plato and now thought spurious.

Axiochus.who: Axiochus, Athenian and uncle of Alcibiades, whom Socrates comforts against the fear of death in the pseudo-Platonic Axiochus.

Axion.who: Axion, son of Phegeus of Psophis in myth, who with his brother dedicated the necklace of Harmonia at Delphi.

Axius.who: The Axius, now the Vardar, the chief river of Macedonia, which flows into the Gulf of Thessaloniki.

Axylos.who: Axylus, son of Teuthras, a wealthy and hospitable Trojan ally in Iliad 6 who kept open house by the road and was killed by Diomedes.

Azores.who: The Azores, Portuguese islands in the mid-Atlantic.

Azorius.who: Juan Azor (1535–1603), Spanish Jesuit moral theologian, author of the Institutiones morales on cases of conscience.

B. Holiday.who: Barten Holyday (1593–1661), English clergyman and translator, whose allegorical comedy Technogamia was acted at Oxford in 1618.

Baal.who: Baal, the chief storm and fertility god of the Canaanites and Phoenicians, whose cult the Old Testament prophets condemned.

Babel.who: Babel, the city whose tower in Genesis 11 led to the confusion of tongues.

Babylon.who: Babylon, the ancient capital of Babylonia on the Euphrates, in modern Iraq, famous for its hanging gardens.

Babylon. Commodus.basis: The form wrongly joins 'Babylon' to 'Commodus', which begins the next sentence; this entry identifies only Babylon.
Babylon. Commodus.who: Babylon, the ancient capital of Babylonia on the Euphrates, in modern Iraq.

Babylonian.who: Refers to the 'goodly Babylonish garment' that Achan stole with silver and a wedge of gold at the fall of Jericho (Joshua 7:21).

Babylonian Thisbe.who: Thisbe, the Babylonian girl loved by Pyramus, whose tragic story Ovid tells in Metamorphoses 4.

Babylonians.who: The Babylonians, the ancient inhabitants of Babylon and Babylonia in Mesopotamia.

Bacchi.who: Bacchus (Latin genitive), the Roman god of wine; Florus calls Campania a 'contest of Bacchus and Venus'.

Bacchon.basis: The story of Ismenodora and Bacchon is in Plutarch's Amatorius, not in Pausanias as Burton cites it.
Bacchon.who: Bacchon, a handsome youth of Thespiae whom the wealthy widow Ismenodora carried off and married, as told in Plutarch's Amatorius.

Bacchus.who: Bacchus (Dionysus), the Greco-Roman god of wine, also called Liber pater.

Bacchus. Cotys.basis: The form wrongly joins 'Bacchus' to 'Cotys', which begins the next sentence; this entry identifies only Bacchus.
Bacchus. Cotys.who: Bacchus (Dionysus), the god of wine, whom Mark Antony impersonated at Alexandria.

Backward.basis: A heading in an anatomical division, not a name.

Bacon.basis: The second passage is a marginal citation of Francis Bacon's essay on marriage and single life.
Bacon.who: First passage: Roger Bacon (c.1219–c.1292), English Franciscan natural philosopher. Second: Francis Bacon (1561–1626), quoted from his Essays.

Baconthorpe.who: John Baconthorpe (c.1290–1346), English Carmelite scholastic theologian, known as 'Doctor Resolutus'.

Bacon’s Essays.who: The Essays of Francis Bacon (1561–1626), first published 1597 and enlarged in 1612 and 1625.

Bactriana.who: Bactria, the ancient region between the Hindu Kush and the Oxus, in modern northern Afghanistan and neighbouring lands; Burton equates it with Khorasan.

Bad.basis: The ordinary word 'bad', used of the passions.

Baden.who: Baden in Aargau, Switzerland, a spa town whose mixed public baths Poggio Bracciolini described in a famous letter.

Baiae.who: Baiae, a luxurious Roman seaside resort on the Bay of Naples, near modern Baia in Campania.

Bajazet.basis: Burton calls the first 'the second Emperor'; the captive Bajazet is Bayezid I.
Bajazet.who: First passage: Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II (r. 1481–1512). Others: Bayezid I (r. 1389–1402), defeated and captured by Timur in 1402.

Baldus.basis: The second passage names a mountain, not the lawyer.
Baldus.who: Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), Italian jurist of Perugia; in the second passage, Monte Baldo, a mountain range by Lake Garda (Benacus) famous for medicinal plants.

Bale.who: John Bale (1495–1563), English Protestant polemicist, playwright and bishop of Ossory, who attacked monks and the papacy and wrote catalogues of British writers.

Baleum.basis: Baleum is a Latin form of Bale.
Baleum.who: John Bale (1495–1563), English Protestant polemicist and bishop of Ossory, author of an anti-papal history of the Roman pontiffs.

Ballad.basis: An ordinary word; 'Ballad of Ballads' is an old English title for the Song of Songs.

Ballads.basis: An ordinary word; part of 'Ballad of Ballads'.

Ballio.who: Ballio, the shameless pimp in Plautus's comedy Pseudolus.

Balneum Dianae.basis: Name of a Paracelsian remedy ('Bath of Diana'); not certain what it was.

Balthasar Castilio.who: Baldassare Castiglione (1478–1529), Italian courtier and diplomat, author of The Book of the Courtier (Il Cortegiano, 1528).

Baltic.who: The Baltic Sea in northern Europe.

Bamberg.who: Bamberg, a city in Franconia, Germany, then the seat of a powerful prince-bishopric.

Banbury.who: Banbury, a market town in north Oxfordshire, then famous for its cheese.

Bang.basis: The spelling and the account of its effects fit bhang.
Bang.who: Bhang, an Indian intoxicating preparation of cannabis leaves, which Garcia da Orta described.

Banians.who: The Banians (Baniyas), Hindu and Jain merchant castes of Gujarat, noted by European travellers for refusing to eat flesh or kill animals.

Bannockburn.who: Bannockburn, near Stirling, Scotland, where Robert the Bruce defeated Edward II in 1314.

Banquo.who: Banquo, a legendary Scottish thane in Hector Boece's chronicle, held to be the ancestor of the Stuarts and later a character in Shakespeare's Macbeth.

Bantam.who: Bantam (Banten), a pepper port in western Java, Indonesia, where the English East India Company had a trading post from 1602.

Baptista Codronchus.who: Giovanni Battista Codronchi (1547–1628), physician of Imola, author of a commentary on white hellebore and a treatise on rabies.

Baptista Morinus.who: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583–1656), French mathematician and astrologer who attacked the Copernican system, including Lansbergen's defence of it.

Baptista Porta.who: Giambattista della Porta (c.1535–1615), Neapolitan natural philosopher, author of Magia naturalis and works on physiognomy and optics.

Baptista Turrianus.basis: Fracastoro's friend of this name fits the Latin form; dates left out as uncertain.
Baptista Turrianus.who: Giovanni Battista della Torre, Veronese physician and astronomer, a friend of Girolamo Fracastoro, who named a dialogue after him.

Baraballius.who: Giacomo Baraballo, abbot of Gaeta, a vain poetaster whom Pope Leo X mockingly 'crowned' as poet laureate in 1514, parading him on the elephant Hanno.

Barbarian.who: Generic term for a foreigner, originally anyone not Greek or Roman.

Barbarians.who: In Greek and Roman usage, all non-Greek or non-Roman peoples; in the Britons' complaint, the Picts and Scots.

Barbary.who: Barbary, the Mediterranean coast of North Africa (modern Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya).

Barbiccians.who: The Derbices, an ancient Central Asian people near the Caspian, said by Aelian (Varia Historia 4.1) to kill their old people over seventy.

Barcino.who: Barcino, the Latin name of Barcelona in Catalonia.

Baricellus.who: Giulio Cesare Barricelli, early 17th-century south Italian physician, author of the miscellany Hortus genialis (1620).

Barletius.who: Marin Barleti (c.1450–c.1512), Albanian humanist priest of Shkodër, author of a Latin life of Scanderbeg.

Barocius.who: Francesco Barozzi (1537–1604), Venetian nobleman and mathematician, whose Cosmographia (1585) listed errors in Sacrobosco's Sphere.

Baronius.basis: The second and third passages cite the Annales; the first is a marginal citation of 'Justus Baronius', a different writer.
Baronius.who: Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), Italian cardinal and church historian, author of the Annales Ecclesiastici.

Barradius.who: Sebastião Barradas (1543–1615), Portuguese Jesuit, author of commentaries on the harmony of the Gospels.

Barrowists.who: Followers of Henry Barrow (c.1550–1593), English Separatist Puritan executed for sedition.

Barry.who: Barry Island, off the Glamorgan coast in the Bristol Channel, Wales.

Barthius Celestina.who: Caspar Barth's (1587–1658) Latin translation of the Spanish Celestina, published as Pornoboscodidascalus (1624).

Bartholomaeus Anglicus.who: Bartholomaeus Anglicus (13th century), English Franciscan, author of the encyclopedia De proprietatibus rerum.

Bartholomaeus à Casa.who: Bartolomé de las Casas (1484–1566), Spanish Dominican, bishop of Chiapas, who denounced Spanish cruelty to the American Indians.

Bartholus.who: Bartolus of Sassoferrato (1313/14–1357), the most famous Italian jurist and commentator on Roman law.

Bartison.who: Willem Barentsz (c.1550–1597), Dutch navigator who sought a northern passage and wintered on Novaya Zemlya in 1596–97.

Bartolus.who: Bartolus of Sassoferrato (1313/14–1357), the most famous Italian jurist and commentator on Roman law.

Basel.who: Basel, city on the Rhine in Switzerland.

Basel Anno.who: Basel, city on the Rhine in Switzerland.

Bashaws.who: Pashas, high-ranking Ottoman governors and military commanders.

Basil.who: St Basil the Great (c.330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Greek Church Father.

Basilidean.who: Followers of Basilides, 2nd-century Gnostic teacher at Alexandria.

Bassa.who: Pasha, title of a high-ranking Ottoman governor or commander.

Bath.who: Bath, city in Somerset, England, home of Chaucer's Wife of Bath.

Bathsheba.who: Bathsheba, wife of Uriah, whom King David saw bathing and took; mother of Solomon (2 Samuel 11).

Bathyllus.who: Bathyllus, beautiful Samian youth loved and praised by the Greek lyric poet Anacreon.

Battle Abbey.who: Battle Abbey, Sussex, founded by William the Conqueror on the site of the Battle of Hastings (1066).

Bauhinus.who: Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), Swiss anatomist and botanist of Basel, author of the Theatrum anatomicum and the Pinax.
