Baume.who: Sainte-Baume, grotto and pilgrimage site of Mary Magdalene in Provence, where Madeleine de Demandolx was exorcised in 1610–11.

Bavarian.who: Of Bavaria, the duchy in southern Germany.

Bavarians.who: Inhabitants of Bavaria in southern Germany.

Bavius.who: Bavius (d. 35 BC), bad Roman poet mocked with Mevius by Virgil (Eclogue 3), a byword for poetasters.

Bayard.who: Bayard, the legendary magic horse of the Charlemagne romances; 'bold as blind Bayard' was proverbial for reckless ignorance.

Bayrus.who: Pietro Bairo (Petrus Bayrus, 1468–1558), physician of Turin, author of a handbook of remedies popularly called the *Veni mecum*.

Beatrice.who: Beatrice, the witty heroine of Shakespeare's *Much Ado About Nothing*, who quarrels with Benedick and then falls in love with him.

Bebelius.basis: The Latin form and the context of humanist Latin versions of Boccaccio fit Bebel.
Bebelius.who: Heinrich Bebel (1472–1518), German humanist Latin poet and professor at Tübingen.

Bedlam.who: Bethlem (Bethlehem) Hospital in London, the hospital for the insane.

Bedmar.who: Alfonso de la Cueva, Marquess of Bedmar (1572–1655), Spanish ambassador at Venice, to whom García de Silva y Figueroa wrote from Isfahan in 1619.

Beelzebub.who: Beelzebub, the Philistine god of Ekron, called in the Gospels the prince of devils.

Beemster.who: The Beemster, a lake in North Holland that was drained and turned into a polder in 1612.

Bel.who: Bel, the chief god of Babylon (Marduk), known from the apocryphal story of Bel and the Dragon.

Belgian.basis: An Asian desert named with Lop, apparently taken from travel accounts; cannot be identified with certainty.

Beli.who: Bel, the chief god of Babylon (Marduk).

Belial.who: Belial, a biblical name for worthlessness, later used as the name of a devil or a prince of devils.

Bellantius.who: Lucio Bellanti (d. 1499), astrologer of Siena, who defended astrology against Pico della Mirandola.

Bellarmine.who: Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), Italian Jesuit cardinal and leading Catholic controversialist.

Bellerophon.who: Bellerophon, Greek hero, falsely accused by Stheneboea; in Homer he ends up wandering alone and melancholy.

Bellonius.who: Pierre Belon (1517–1564), French naturalist who travelled in Greece and the Levant and wrote the *Observations* on them.

Bellovacus.basis: A physician cited from Trincavelli's consilia; the Latin name ('of Beauvais') does not settle who he is.

Belus.who: Belus: in the first passage, the mythical king of Egypt and father of Danaus; in the second, the legendary Assyrian king linked with Semiramis.

Belvedere.who: The Belvedere, the papal villa and garden court in the Vatican, Rome.

Belvoir.who: Belvoir Castle, the hilltop seat of the Earls of Rutland in Leicestershire.

Bembus.who: Pietro Bembo (1470–1547), Venetian cardinal and humanist, author of a Latin history of Venice.

Benacus.who: Lacus Benacus, the Latin name of Lake Garda in northern Italy.

Benedetto Varchi.who: Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), Florentine humanist and historian, who wrote a lecture on jealousy.

Benedick.who: Benedick, the sworn bachelor in Shakespeare's *Much Ado About Nothing*, who quarrels with Beatrice and then falls in love with her.

Benedict.who: First passage: Bento de Góis (1562–1607), Portuguese Jesuit who travelled overland from the Mughal court to China. Second: St Benedict of Nursia, founder of Western monasticism.

Benedictus Justinianus.who: Benedetto Giustiniani (d. 1622), Genoese Jesuit theologian, author of commentaries on the Pauline epistles.

Benedictus Victorius Faventinus.who: Benedetto Vettori of Faenza (1481–1561), Italian physician who taught at Padua and wrote the *Empirica*, a collection of remedies.

Benevenius. Anthony Benevenius.who: Antonio Benivieni (1443–1502), Florentine physician, author of *De abditis morborum causis*, an early book of case histories.

Beneventinus.who: Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556), archbishop of Benevento, poet and author of the *Galateo*, notorious for an obscene comic poem.

Benius.who: Paolo Beni (c.1552–1625), Italian humanist who wrote a commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*.

Benzo.who: Girolamo Benzoni (b. c.1519), Milanese traveller, author of the *Historia del Mondo Nuovo* (1565) about the Spanish Americas.

Benzonus.who: Girolamo Benzoni (b. c.1519), Milanese traveller, author of the *Historia del Mondo Nuovo* (1565) about the Spanish Americas.

Berengarius.who: Berengar of Tours (c.999–1088), French theologian known for his dispute over the Eucharist, commemorated in verse by Hildebert of Lavardin.

Berenice.who: Berenice Syra, daughter of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, married to the Seleucid king Antiochus II.

Bergamo.who: Bergamo, a city in Lombardy in northern Italy.

Bergen.basis: Could be Bergen in Norway (a Hanseatic staple) or Bergen-op-Zoom (famous for its fairs); the passage does not decide.

Berkeley.who: First two passages: George, 8th Baron Berkeley (1601–1658), Burton's patron, who presented him to Segrave. Third: Berkeley, a town in Gloucestershire.

Berkshire.who: Berkshire, county of southern England, in which Wadley (near Faringdon) lies.

Bernadinus Scardeonius.who: Bernardino Scardeone (1478–1574), Paduan canon and historian, author of De antiquitate urbis Patavii et claris civibus Patavinis.

Bernard Canisianus.basis: Ficino's letters include several to Bernardo Canigiani; Burton's form is a garbled Latinisation
Bernard Canisianus.who: Bernardo Canigiani, Florentine friend and correspondent of Marsilio Ficino.

Bernardinus Telesius.who: Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), Italian natural philosopher of Cosenza whose De rerum natura attacked Aristotle's physics.

Bernardinus de Bustis.who: Bernardino de' Busti (c. 1450–c. 1513), Italian Franciscan preacher, author of the Rosarium sermonum and the Mariale.

Bernardus Paternus.who: Bernardino Paterno, sixteenth-century Italian physician who taught medicine at Padua; Hildesheim's Spicilegia print his consultations.

Bernardus Penottus.who: Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1519–1617), French Paracelsian physician and alchemist, author of the Denarius medicus.

Berne.who: Bern, city and canton in Switzerland.

Beroaldus.who: Filippo Beroaldo the Elder (1453–1505), humanist of Bologna, commentator on Apuleius and author of a tract on earthquakes and plague.

Berosus.who: Berossus (fl. early 3rd century BC), Babylonian priest and historian; the work cited was the forgery published under his name by Annius of Viterbo.

Bertius.who: Petrus Bertius (1565–1629), Flemish geographer and cartographer, author of works on the geography of Germany and the Low Countries.

Besardus.who: Jean-Baptiste Besard (c. 1567–after 1617), physician and lutenist of Besançon, author of the medical compendium Antrum philosophicum.

Besardus Vesontinus.who: Jean-Baptiste Besard of Besançon (c. 1567–after 1617), physician and lutenist, author of the Antrum philosophicum.

Besler.who: Basilius Besler (1561–1629), Nuremberg apothecary who published the great illustrated florilegium Hortus Eystettensis (1613).

Bess.who: A generic pet name for Elizabeth, in an alliterative list of stock girls' names.

Bethesda.who: Bethesda, the healing pool in Jerusalem where an angel troubled the water (John 5).

Beza.who: Theodore Beza (1519–1605), French Reformed theologian, Calvin's successor at Geneva, author of a treatise on divorce and of a defence of punishing heretics.

Bezoar.who: Bezoar stone, an animal concretion used as an antidote.

Biarmi.basis: Varthema's account of the Calicut kings and the priests who deflower their wives; Biarmi looks like a corruption of Brahmini
Biarmi.who: The Brahmins, the priestly caste of Calicut as described by Ludovico di Varthema.

Biarmia.who: Bjarmaland (Biarmia), region of the far north of Russia around the White Sea.

Bias.who: Bias of Priene (6th century BC), one of the Seven Sages of Greece.

Bibienna.who: Bernardo Dovizi da Bibbiena (1470–1520), cardinal and confidant of Pope Leo X, author of the comedy Calandria.

Biermannus.basis: named among Weyer-style sceptics of witchcraft; the Latin form fits Biermann's Helmstedt treatise
Biermannus.who: Martin Biermann, German physician who wrote De magicis actionibus (1590), sceptical of witches' powers.

Bilia.who: Bilia, wife of the Roman consul Gaius Duilius (3rd century BC), praised for chastity in the anecdote of his bad breath.

Bilibaldus Pirkimerus.who: Willibald Pirckheimer (1470–1530), Nuremberg humanist and councillor, long crippled by gout, author of a mock praise of gout.

Bion.who: Bion of Borysthenes (c. 325–c. 255 BC), Cynic philosopher who spoke openly of his freedman father and courtesan mother.

Bishoprics.who: Bishoprics, i.e. bishops' sees as church offices.

Bithynia.who: Bithynia, ancient region of north-western Asia Minor on the Black Sea and Sea of Marmara, now in Turkey.

Bitias.who: Bitias, a Tyrian guest at Dido's banquet in Virgil's Aeneid (Book 1) who drains the brimming wine-cup.

Blancanus.who: Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), Jesuit mathematician of Bologna, author of Echometria and of a work on the mathematical passages in Aristotle.

Blandamour.who: Sir Blandamour, a knight in Book 4 of Spenser's Faerie Queene who fights Paridell over Florimel.

Blase.who: St Blaise (d. c. 316), bishop of Sebaste and martyr, whose feast (3 February) was kept with popular ceremonies.

Blasius.basis: a Christian reporter of the 1596 Japanese earthquake; not securely identifiable

Blondus.who: Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), Italian humanist historian and antiquary, author of Italia illustrata.

Blood.who: Blood, one of the four humours.

Boaz.who: Boaz, kinsman of Naomi who married Ruth in the Book of Ruth.

Boccace.who: Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), Italian writer, author of the Decameron.

Boccalinus.who: Traiano Boccalini (1556–1613), Italian satirist, author of the *Ragguagli di Parnaso* (Advertisements from Parnassus), in which Apollo hears complaints and judges states.

Bocchoris.who: Bocchoris (Bakenranef), pharaoh of Egypt's 24th dynasty (late 8th century BC), remembered by Greek writers as a lawgiver.

Bocerus.basis: A German Latin poet of this name is known; I cannot confirm that his poem on the Freiburg plays is the one cited.

Bodecheri Sat.who: Benjamin Bodecher Banning, Dutch neo-Latin poet, author of a *Satyricon* (1615) of Latin satires.

Boedina.who: Boidion, an Athenian courtesan whom Plutarch names among the women in Epicurus' circle.

Boeotian Thebes.who: Thebes in Boeotia, central Greece, as distinct from Egyptian Thebes.

Boeotians.who: The inhabitants of Boeotia in central Greece, whom other Greeks proverbially called dull-witted.

Boeth.who: Boethius (c. 480–524), Roman philosopher and statesman; the verse quoted opens his *Consolation of Philosophy*.

Boethius.who: Boethius (c. 480–524), Roman philosopher, author of *The Consolation of Philosophy* and *De institutione musica*.

Bohemia.who: Bohemia, a kingdom of central Europe, now the western part of the Czech Republic.

Bohemian.who: Of Bohemia, now the western Czech Republic.

Bohemians.who: The people of Bohemia, now the western Czech Republic.

Bohemus de Turcis.who: Johann Boemus (c. 1485–1535), German humanist, author of *Omnium gentium mores*, an account of the customs of the world's peoples, including the Turks.

Bologna.who: Bologna, a university city of northern Italy.

Bolton.who: Robert Bolton (1572–1631), English Puritan divine, author of *Instructions for a Right Comforting Afflicted Consciences*.

Bombomachides.who: Bumbomachides, the absurdly named enemy general whom the braggart soldier claims to have beaten in Plautus' *Miles Gloriosus*; here a type of the swaggerer.

Bonaciolus.who: Lodovico Bonaccioli (fl. c. 1500), physician at Ferrara, author of *Enneas muliebris*, a treatise on women's bodies and childbirth.

Bonaventure.who: St Bonaventure (1221–1274), Franciscan theologian and cardinal; the *Dieta salutis* was attributed to him.

Bonifacius.who: St Boniface (c. 675–754), English missionary and archbishop of Mainz, who accused Virgil of Salzburg of believing in the Antipodes.

Bononia.who: Bononia, the Latin name of Bologna in northern Italy.

Bononian.who: Of Bologna (Latin Bononia), whose university employed Filippo Beroaldo the Elder as a professor.

Bonosi.who: Bonosus (d. c. 281), Roman usurper on the Rhine under Probus, notorious as a huge drinker.

Bonosus.who: Bonosus (d. c. 281), Roman usurper on the Rhine under Probus, notorious as a huge drinker.

Boreas.who: Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind.

Borneo.who: Borneo, the large island of the East Indies, then also the name of its sultanate (Brunei).

Bosnia.who: Bosnia, in the Balkans, then under Ottoman rule.

Botallus.who: Leonardo Botallo (1530–c. 1587), Piedmontese physician to the French court, author of *De lue venerea* on syphilis.

Boter.who: Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617), Italian political writer, author of the *Relazioni universali*, a description of the world's states.

Boterus Amphitheatridion.who: Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617), Italian political writer; his *Amphitheatridion* is a Latin work of political and historical reflections.

Bourbon.who: Charles de Bourbon (1433–1488), cardinal and archbishop of Lyon, whom Louis XI jokingly offered as confessor to Edward IV (Commines).

Bourbonian.who: The French royal house of Bourbon, after which Jean Tarde named the sunspots he took for new planets 'Borbonia sidera' (1620).

Bourbourg.who: Bourbourg, a town in French Flanders, near Dunkirk.

Bourges.who: Bourges, a university city in central France.

Boyards.who: Matteo Maria Boiardo (1441–1494), Italian poet, author of the chivalric romance *Orlando innamorato*.

Bozius.basis: His works cover both Roman antiquity and the defence of religion, which fits both passages, but his brother Francesco Bozio also wrote.
Bozius.who: Tommaso Bozio (1548–1610), Italian Oratorian, who wrote on ancient and modern Italy and attacked Machiavelli and 'impious politicians'.

Brabant.who: Brabant, a duchy of the Low Countries, now divided between Belgium and the Netherlands.

Brachmanni.who: The Brahmins, the priestly and learned caste of India, whom Greek and Latin writers called Brachmanes.

Bradford.who: John Bradford (c.1510–1555), English Protestant preacher and Marian martyr, whose letters and treatises comforted troubled consciences.

Bradiopepsia.who: Bradypepsia: slow or weak digestion, a medical term.

Braga.who: Braga, an ancient cathedral city in northern Portugal.

Brain.who: The brain, one of the three principal organs.

Branchus.who: Branchus, in Greek legend a son or favourite of Apollo, given prophecy by the god and founder of the oracle at Didyma near Miletus.

Brande.basis: a physician consulted with Solenander; not otherwise known to me

Brandimarte.who: Brandimarte, a knight in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, Orlando's friend, killed in the battle on Lampedusa against the African kings.

Brasavola.who: Antonio Musa Brasavola (1500–1555), physician of Ferrara, author of an examination of simple medicines and a noted user of hellebore.

Brasidas.who: Brasidas (d. 422 BC), Spartan general in the Peloponnesian War, killed winning the battle of Amphipolis.

Braunus.who: Georg Braun (1541–1622), Cologne cleric who edited the Civitates orbis terrarum, the great atlas of town views, with the engraver Frans Hogenberg.

Brazil.who: Brazil, the Portuguese territory in South America.

Breaute.who: Pierre de Bréauté (d. 1600), French captain in Dutch service, killed after a famous cavalry combat of 22 a side near 's-Hertogenbosch in 1600.

Bremen.who: Bremen, city in northern Germany and seat of a prince-archbishopric.

Brennus.who: Brennus, Gaulish chieftain who led the invasion of Greece and the attack on Delphi in 279 BC. Not the Brennus who sacked Rome.

Brentius.who: Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), Lutheran reformer of Württemberg, author of homilies on the Gospel of Luke.

Breslau.who: Breslau (Latin Vratislavia), capital of Silesia, now Wrocław in Poland.

Breton.who: A Breton, a native of Brittany.

Breydenbach.who: Bernhard von Breydenbach (c.1440–1497), dean of Mainz, author of the illustrated Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam (1486), an account of his pilgrimage.

Bridget.who: In the first passage, St Bridget (Birgitta) of Sweden (c.1303–1373), visionary whose Revelations were read as prophecy. In the second, only a common girl's name.

Briggs.who: Henry Briggs (1561–1630), English mathematician whose map of North America (1625) showed California as an island.

Bright.who: Timothy Bright (c.1551–1615), English physician, author of A Treatise of Melancholy (1586).

Brise.who: Breeze: the cooling trade winds of the tropics.

Briseis.who: Briseis, Achilles' captive concubine in the Iliad, whose seizure by Agamemnon caused Achilles' wrath.

Bristol.who: Bristol, port city in south-west England.

Britain.who: Britain. In the third passage ('Duke of Britain') it means Brittany in north-west France.

Britannos.who: Latin 'the Britons', the English people of Augustine of Canterbury's mission.

British.who: British: of Britain or the ancient Britons.

Briton.who: Of the ancient Britons, here describing the British Druids.

Briton Druids.who: The Druids, priests and teachers of the ancient Celtic Britons and Gauls.

Britons.who: The Britons, the Celtic inhabitants of Britain before the Anglo-Saxons, and their descendants.

Brixia.who: Brixia, now Brescia in Lombardy, then under Venetian rule.

Brocard.who: Burchard of Mount Sion (fl. 1280s), Dominican friar who wrote a widely read Descriptio Terrae Sanctae.

Brontes.who: Brontes, one of the Cyclopes who forged in Vulcan's smithy; here a byword for a sooty blacksmith.

Brotheus.who: Brotheas, a son of Vulcan who threw himself into the fire because he was mocked for his ugliness (Ovid, Ibis).

Brownists.who: Brownists, English Separatists who followed Robert Browne (c.1550–1633) in rejecting the established Church.

Bruele.who: Gualtherus Bruele (Walter Bruel), Flemish physician, author of a Praxis medicinae, a handbook of medical practice.

Bruges.who: Bruges, trading city in Flanders, now in Belgium.

Brundisium.who: Brundisium, now Brindisi, port in Apulia in south-east Italy.

Brundusinus.basis: He was the cardinal known by his see of Brindisi, and this two-line epitaph is attributed to him.
Brundusinus.who: Girolamo Aleandro (1480–1542), humanist, archbishop of Brindisi and cardinal, buried in Rome under an epitaph he wrote himself.

Brunehaut.who: Brunhilda (c.543–613), Visigothic princess and Merovingian queen of Austrasia, famous for her long feud with Fredegund.

Brunner.who: Balthasar Brunner (1533–1604), German physician of Halle, whose *Consilia medica* were published after his death in 1617.

Bruno Seidelius.who: Bruno Seidel (c. 1530–1591), German physician and Latin poet, author of a book on the causes of incurable diseases.

Brunsellius.basis: known only as a case reported by Wolfius

Brunus.who: Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), Italian philosopher who taught an infinite universe with many worlds; burned at Rome for heresy.

Brussels.who: Brussels, chief city of Brabant in the Spanish Netherlands, now the capital of Belgium.

Brutius.basis: named with Bruno as asserting inhabited worlds among the fixed stars; bearer unclear

Brutus.who: Marcus Junius Brutus (85–42 BC), Caesar's assassin, who killed himself after defeat at Philippi.

Bubastis.who: Bubastis, ancient Egyptian city in the Nile delta and centre of the cat-goddess Bastet's cult; now Tell Basta near Zagazig.

Bucer.who: Martin Bucer (1491–1551), Protestant reformer of Strasbourg, who ended his life as a professor at Cambridge.

Bulco Opoliensis.basis: Opoliensis = of Opole; several dukes named Bolko ruled there, so which one is not certain
Bulco Opoliensis.who: Bolko, a Piast duke of Opole (Oppeln) in Silesia in the fifteenth century, described by Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini in his *Europa*.

Bulgary.who: Bulgaria, then a province of the Ottoman Empire.

Bullinger.who: Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), Swiss reformer who succeeded Zwingli as chief minister of Zurich.

Bunduica.who: Boudica (Boadicea; d. c. AD 61), queen of the Iceni, who led a British revolt against Roman rule.

Burbonius.who: Charles III, Duke of Bourbon (1490–1527), Constable of France who went over to Charles V; he was killed leading the imperial army against Rome in 1527.

Burchardus.basis: he is named among Catholic canonists and casuists blamed for explicit writing, which fits Burchard's penitential
Burchardus.who: Burchard of Worms (c. 965–1025), bishop whose *Decretum* includes a penitential that questions in detail about sexual sins.

Burchet.basis: Camden's Annals is cited; 'burned at Norwich' really fits Hamont (Hovatus), and Burton seems to have run the two together
Burchet.who: Peter Burchet (d. 1573), Puritan fanatic who, believing himself inspired, stabbed John Hawkins in London; he is recorded in Camden's Annals.

Burggravius.basis: the context is Rosicrucian and Paracelsian marvels, and the Latin form fits
Burggravius.who: Johann Ernst Burggrav, German Paracelsian physician of the early seventeenth century, who wrote on the sympathetic 'lamp of life'.

Burgos.who: Burgos, city in Old Castile, northern Spain.

Burgundian.who: Burgundy: the reference is to Pontus Heuterus's history of the Burgundian dukes and the Netherlands.

Burgundy.who: The duchy of Burgundy in eastern France, whose Valois dukes, including Charles the Bold, also ruled the Low Countries.

Busbequium.who: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq (1522–1592), Flemish diplomat and imperial ambassador to Suleiman the Magnificent, author of the *Turkish Letters*.

Buscodnese.basis: the form looks like a garbled Buscoducensis, and the physician of Delft is Forestus
Buscodnese.who: Probably not a surname at all: a Carthusian from 's-Hertogenbosch (Latin *Buscoducensis*), a case reported by the Dutch physician Pieter van Foreest.

Busiris.who: Busiris, mythical Egyptian king who sacrificed strangers and was killed by Hercules.

Byzance.who: Byzantium, the Greek city on the Bosporus, later Constantinople and now Istanbul.

Cabeus.who: Niccolò Cabeo (1586–1650), Italian Jesuit natural philosopher, author of *Philosophia magnetica* (1629).

Cabinet du Roy.who: *Le Cabinet du Roy de France* (1581), an anonymous Huguenot satire on the state of France and the vices of its clergy and provinces.

Cabrieres.who: Cabrières-d'Avignon, a Waldensian village in Provence whose people were massacred with those of Mérindol in 1545.

Cachexia.who: Cachexia, a medical term for a general wasting and bad habit of the body.

Cacochymia.who: Cacochymia, a medical term for a corrupt or vitiated state of the humours.

Cacus.who: Cacus, fire-breathing monster of Roman myth who stole Hercules' cattle and was killed by him on the Aventine.

Cadamustus.who: Alvise Cadamosto (c. 1432–1488), Venetian navigator who explored the West African coast in Portuguese service.

Cadmus Milesius.who: Cadmus of Miletus (the younger), an obscure Greek writer whom the Suda credits with fourteen books on love.

Cadurcum.who: Cahors (Latin Cadurcum), town in Quercy, south-western France.

Cadwallader.who: Cadwaladr ap Cadwallon (d. 7th century), king of Gwynedd, remembered in legend as the last British king.

Caecilianus.who: Caecilian, bishop of Carthage from c. 311, whose disputed election set off the Donatist schism.

Caecilius.who: In passages 1 and 3, Caecilius Statius (d. c. 168 BC), Roman comic poet; in passage 2, Caecilius Natalis, the pagan speaker in Minucius Felix's *Octavius*.

Caecina.who: Aulus Caecina Alienus (d. AD 79), Vitellian general famous for his showy dress, later put to death for conspiracy under Vespasian.

Caelia.basis: a stock name for a mistress in poems and romances; different bearers

Caelius.who: In passages 1 and 2, Caelius Rhodiginus (Lodovico Ricchieri, 1469–1525), author of *Lectiones antiquae*; in passage 3, Celio Secondo Curione (1503–1569), Italian Protestant humanist.

Caelius Aurelianus.who: Caelius Aurelianus (fl. 5th century), Latin medical writer from Sicca in Numidia, whose works on acute and chronic diseases adapt Soranus.

Caelius Secundus.who: Celio Secondo Curione (1503–1569), Italian Protestant humanist and religious exile in Basel, author of consolatory and theological works.

Caernarvon.who: Caernarfon, town and castle in north-west Wales, birthplace in 1284 of Edward II, hence 'Edward of Caernarvon'.

Caesar.who: Gaius Julius Caesar (100–44 BC), Roman general and dictator, conqueror of Gaul and rival of Pompey.

Caesar Augustus.who: Augustus (63 BC–AD 14), first Roman emperor, whose physician was Antonius Musa.

Caesar Claudinus.who: Giulio Cesare Claudini (1550–1618), physician and professor at Bologna, author of collected medical consultations.

Caesar Vaninus.who: Giulio Cesare Vanini (1585–1619), Italian naturalist philosopher, author of the dialogues De admirandis naturae arcanis (1616); burned for atheism at Toulouse.

Caesars.who: Julius Caesar and the Roman emperors who succeeded him, whose lives Suetonius and Dio wrote; also used generically for great conquerors.

Caesius.basis: Cesi is the Latin Caesius; which Cesi cardinal is meant is not certain.
Caesius.who: A sixteenth-century cardinal of the Roman Cesi family, patient of the physician Prospero Calanio, to whom his treatise De atra bile was addressed.

Caieta.who: Gaeta, coastal town in southern Lazio, Italy; Baraballo of Gaeta was the poet mocked at the court of Leo X.

Cain.who: Cain, eldest son of Adam and Eve, who murdered his brother Abel (Genesis 4).

Cajetan.who: Tommaso de Vio, Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), Dominican theologian and Thomist commentator, author of commentaries on the Psalms and other scripture.

Cajetanus.who: Cardinal Bonifazio Caetani (1567–1617), to whom Tommaso Campanella dedicated his Apologia pro Galileo.

Calabria.who: Calabria, region forming the toe of southern Italy.

Calabrian.who: A native of Calabria in southern Italy; Campanella was born at Stilo there.

Calais.who: First, Calais, the French port besieged by Edward III in 1347; second, Calais, winged son of Boreas and Orithyia, brother of Zetes and an Argonaut.

Calanius.who: Prospero Calanio (Calani), sixteenth-century Italian physician, author of a treatise De atra bile on melancholy.

Calanus.who: Calanus, Indian gymnosophist who followed Alexander the Great and burned himself alive on a pyre in Persia, c. 323 BC.

Calasiris.who: Calasiris, the aged Egyptian priest of Isis in Heliodorus's romance the Aethiopica.

Calcagninus Apol.who: Celio Calcagnini (1479–1541), humanist of Ferrara, whose Apologi are a collection of moral fables.

Calcagninus Apologis.who: Celio Calcagnini (1479–1541), humanist of Ferrara, whose Apologi are a collection of moral fables.

Calchas.who: Calchas, the Greek seer at Troy who demanded the sacrifice of Iphigenia.

Caleb.who: Caleb, with Joshua the only faithful spy sent into Canaan who entered the Promised Land (Numbers 13–14).

Caledonian.who: Of Caledonia, the Roman name for northern Britain; the lady is Argentocoxus's wife, whose retort to Julia Domna is recorded by Cassius Dio.

Calenders.who: Qalandars, wandering mendicant dervishes of the Islamic world.

Calicut.who: Calicut, modern Kozhikode, port on the Malabar coast of Kerala, south-west India.

California.who: California, on the Pacific coast of North America, wrongly shown as an island on seventeenth-century maps.

Caligula.who: Caligula (Gaius, AD 12–41), Roman emperor; Suetonius reports his gibe that Seneca's style was 'sand without lime'.

Calisto.who: Calisto, the young lover of Melibea in Fernando de Rojas's Spanish tragicomedy La Celestina (1499).

Callias.basis: Named among Socrates' contemporaries and interlocutors; he is the best-known Callias in that circle.
Callias.who: Callias (c. 450–370 BC), wealthy Athenian patron of the sophists, host in Plato's Protagoras and Xenophon's Symposium.

Callicratidas.who: First, apparently Callicrates, architect of the Parthenon, misnamed by Burton; second and third, Callicratidas, the lover of women who speaks in the Lucianic dialogue Amores.

Callides.basis: The courtesan's advice and the rich suitor Demophantus match Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.
Callides.who: Callides, a painter used to make a lover jealous, in one of Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Callimachus.who: Callimachus (c. 310–c. 240 BC), Alexandrian poet and scholar, who said 'a big book is a big evil' and wrote the epigram on Cleombrotus of Ambracia.

Calliopius.who: Calliopius, late-antique editor of Terence's comedies, whose subscription 'Calliopius recensui' ends the plays in manuscripts.

Callirhoe.who: Callirhoe, maiden of Calydon loved by the priest Coresus, who sacrificed himself in her place, as told by Pausanias, book 7.

Callisthenes.who: Callisthenes of Olynthus (d. 327 BC), Aristotle's kinsman and Alexander the Great's historian, put to death after opposing him.

Callisto.who: Callisto, nymph of Artemis seduced by Zeus and turned into a bear (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2).

Callistratus.who: Callistratus (3rd–4th century AD), Greek sophist, author of the Descriptions (Ekphraseis) of statues.

Calpurnia.who: First, Calpurnia, devoted wife of Pliny the Younger; second, Calpurnia, a noblewoman ruined by Agrippina's jealousy under Claudius (Tacitus, Annals 12).

Calvin.who: John Calvin (1509–1564), French Protestant reformer of Geneva, who had Servetus burned and preached sermons on Job.

Calvinists.who: Followers of John Calvin's Reformed Protestant theology.

Camaepitis.who: Chamaepitys, ground pine (Ajuga chamaepitys), a medicinal herb.

Cambalu.who: Khanbaliq, the Mongol capital of China described by Marco Polo, now Beijing.

Cambray.who: Cambrai, town in northern France, known for its weaving and for the League of Cambrai (1508) formed against Venice.

Cambridge.who: Cambridge, English university town near the Fens.

Cambrioll Colchos.who: Cambriol, the short-lived Welsh colony that William Vaughan founded c. 1617 on the Avalon Peninsula of Newfoundland, promoted in his Golden Fleece (1626).

Cambyses.who: Cambyses I, Persian king and father of Cyrus the Great, who gives his son advice in Xenophon's Cyropaedia.

Camden’s Remains.who: William Camden's Remains Concerning Britain (1605), a miscellany of English antiquities and anecdotes.

Camerarius.basis: The life of Melanchthon is by the elder; the Symbola et emblemata centuries are by the younger; the husbandry reference most likely means the younger.
Camerarius.who: Joachim Camerarius the Elder (1500–1574), Melanchthon's biographer, in the first passage; the emblems are by his son Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a physician and botanist.

Camillus.who: Marcus Furius Camillus (d. c. 365 BC), Roman general and conqueror of Veii, who was exiled by the Romans and later recalled.

Camillus de Camillis.who: Camillo Camilli (fl. 1580s), Italian man of letters, author of Imprese illustri (1586), a book of emblematic devices.

Camoena.who: An Italian girl's name (Latin camena, 'Muse'), cited as one of the pretty names given to fair daughters.

Campanella’s Atheismus Triumphatus.who: Tommaso Campanella's Atheismus triumphatus (Rome, 1631), a refutation of atheism by the Calabrian Dominican philosopher (1568–1639).

Campanian.who: Inhabitants of Campania in southern Italy, chiefly of its capital Capua.

Campaspe.who: Campaspe, mistress of Alexander the Great, who gave her to the painter Apelles when Apelles fell in love with her.

Campian.basis: The Latin jibe at the clergy and the marginal 'Campian' fit the Jesuit; the exact source is not verified.
Campian.who: Edmund Campion (1540–1581), English Jesuit martyr, known for his scornful remarks on the Protestant clergy.

Candaules.who: Candaules, king of Lydia, who showed his naked wife to Gyges and was then killed by him (Herodotus, book 1).

Candish.who: Thomas Cavendish (1560–1592), English navigator and the third man to sail round the world (1586–88).

Canidia.who: Canidia, the witch of Horace's Epodes and Satires.

Cannae.who: Cannae, in Apulia, where Hannibal destroyed a Roman army in 216 BC.

Cannibals.who: Man-eaters; the name originally referred to the Caribs of the West Indies.

Canopus.who: Canopus, ancient Egyptian town near Alexandria, notorious for luxury and licence.

Canossus.who: Canossa, castle in Emilia, northern Italy, where Emperor Henry IV did penance before Pope Gregory VII in 1077.

Cantabria.who: Cantabria, mountainous region of northern Spain.

Canterbury.who: Canterbury in Kent, site of Thomas Becket's shrine and destination of Chaucer's pilgrims.

Canutus.who: Cnut the Great (d. 1035), Danish king of England, said in legend to have fought Edmund Ironside in single combat in 1016.

Cape Verde.who: The Cape Verde Islands, in the Atlantic off West Africa.

Capellanus.basis: He is the best-known love writer of the name, but Burton lists him among modern poets, so another Capellanus is possible.
Capellanus.who: Andreas Capellanus (fl. late 12th century), author of the Latin treatise De amore on courtly love.

Capernaites.basis: The cited 2 Kings 17 gives Adrammelech to the Sepharvites.
Capernaites.who: The Sepharvites of 2 Kings 17:31, who worshipped Adrammelech; 'Capernaites' appears to be Burton's slip.

Cappam.who: Latin cappa, a cloak or cope (here a friar's habit).

Capricorn.who: The Tropic of Capricorn, the parallel at about 23½° south latitude.

Capua.who: Capua, chief city of ancient Campania, whose luxury was said to have softened Hannibal's army.

Capuae Fluenta.who: Aegospotami ('Goat's Rivers'), stream in the Thracian Chersonese where a famous meteorite fell c. 467 BC; Burton's Latin mistranslates the name.

Capuchin.who: A Capuchin friar: a member of the strict reformed branch of the Franciscan order, founded in Italy in the 1520s.

Caracalla.who: Caracalla (188–217), Roman emperor from 198, who murdered his brother Geta and was notorious for cruelty.

Caravans.who: Caravans: armed companies of merchants or pilgrims travelling together across the deserts for protection.

Carbuncle.who: Carbuncle: a red gemstone, such as a garnet or ruby, credited with protective powers.

Cardans.who: Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), Italian physician, mathematician and natural philosopher; the plural means 'men like Cardano'.

Cardinal Caesius.basis: Some cardinal of the Cesi family, but several held the office in the sixteenth century.

Carduus Benedictus.who: Blessed thistle (Cnicus benedictus), a medicinal herb.

Careless.who: John Careless (d. 1556), Coventry weaver and Protestant who died in prison under Mary I; he wrote letters to the martyr John Bradford.

Carew.who: Richard Carew of Antony (1555–1620), Cornish antiquary and author of the Survey of Cornwall (1602).

Caria.who: Caria, an ancient region in south-western Asia Minor (modern south-west Turkey), where Mount Latmos stands.

Carneades.who: Carneades of Cyrene (c. 214–129 BC), sceptical philosopher who headed the Platonic Academy at Athens.

Carniola.who: Carniola, a historic Habsburg duchy now in Slovenia; the lake meant is Lake Cerknica, which fills and drains away.

Carolus Gonzaga.who: Charles I Gonzaga-Nevers (1580–1637), Duke of Nevers, who became Duke of Mantua in 1627.

Carolus Magnus.who: Charlemagne (c. 747–814), king of the Franks and emperor from 800.

Carolus Paschalius.who: Charles Pascal (Carlo Pasquali, 1547–1625), Italian-born humanist and French diplomat, author of a treatise on the virtues and vices.

Carolus Pugnax.who: Charles the Bold (1433–1477), Duke of Burgundy, killed at Nancy; his daughter and heir was Mary of Burgundy.

Carolus Sapiens.who: Charles V 'the Wise' (1338–1380), king of France from 1364.

Carolus à Lorme.basis: The Montpellier degree theses fit Charles de Lorme, but his father Jean was also a physician.
Carolus à Lorme.who: Charles de Lorme (1584–1678), French physician who graduated at Montpellier and was later physician to Louis XIII.

Carotides.who: The carotid arteries of the neck.

Cartarius.who: Vincenzo Cartari (c. 1531–c. 1569), Italian mythographer, author of Le imagini de i dei de gli antichi (1556).

Carthage.who: Carthage, the ancient Phoenician city near modern Tunis, destroyed by Rome in 146 BC.

Carthaginian.who: A native of Carthage in North Africa.

Carthaginians.who: The people of ancient Carthage, Rome's great rival in the Punic Wars.

Carthusians.who: The Carthusians, a strict contemplative monastic order founded by St Bruno in 1084.

Carthusianus.who: Denis the Carthusian (Dionysius Carthusianus, 1402–1471), Flemish mystic theologian and prolific biblical commentator.

Casaubon.who: Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), Genevan-born classical scholar; his Exercitationes (1614) against Baronius denied the authenticity of the Sibylline oracles.

Casaubonus.who: Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), Genevan-born classical scholar and friend of Joseph Scaliger.

Casca.who: 'Old woman', from the old Latin cascus ('old'); the old Roman tag 'cascus cascam ducit' means an old man weds an old woman.

Cascus.who: 'Old man', from the old Latin cascus ('old'); the old Roman tag 'cascus cascam ducit' means an old man weds an old woman.

Casimirus.who: Casimir III the Great (1310–1370), king of Poland, whose second wife was Adelaide of Hesse.

Caspian.who: The Caspian Sea, the inland sea between south-eastern Europe and Central Asia.

Cassandra.who: Cassandra, Trojan princess and prophetess, fated never to be believed.

Cassiopeia.who: The constellation Cassiopeia, where Tycho Brahe's new star appeared in 1572.

Cassius.basis: The first passage means Gaius Cassius Longinus, Caesar's assassin; the Cassius favoured by Vespasian is a different and uncertain person.

Castellio.who: Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), Savoyard humanist and Bible translator, who opposed Calvin over executing heretics and called the Song of Songs a profane love poem.

Castile.who: Castile, the kingdom of central Spain.

Castilians.who: The people of the kingdom of Castile in Spain.

Castor.who: Castor, who with his twin Pollux made up the Dioscuri; their names were also given to St Elmo's fire.

Castruccius Castrucanus.who: Castruccio Castracani (1281–1328), condottiere and lord of Lucca, idealised in Machiavelli's Life of Castruccio Castracani.

Cataia.who: Cathay, the medieval European name for northern China, which Matteo Ricci showed to be the same country as China.

Catalectis.who: The *Catalecta*, a collection of short Latin poems; Scaliger's edition of minor ancient poets included verses attributed to Petronius.

Catalonia.who: Catalonia, region of north-eastern Spain whose chief city is Barcelona (Latin Barcino).

Catanian Philippa.who: Philippa of Catania (d. 1345), a laundress who rose to be governess and confidante of Queen Joanna I of Naples; she was executed after the murder of Joanna's husband Andrew.

Catharine.basis: wife of a Byzantine prince Constantine in Nicephorus Gregoras; I cannot securely identify her

Catherine.who: St Catherine of Alexandria, early Christian virgin martyr broken on the wheel, and so the patron saint of spinners.

Cathesbeius.who: Qaitbay (d. 1496), Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria from 1468, who began life as a Circassian slave.

Catiline.who: Lucius Sergius Catilina (d. 62 BC), Roman nobleman whose conspiracy against the republic was exposed by Cicero and described by Sallust.

Cato.basis: Plutarch's old-ox anecdote is about Cato the Elder; Seneca and Velleius praise Cato of Utica
Cato.who: In the first passage, Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), Roman censor; in the second (and the third's note), his great-grandson Cato the Younger (95–46 BC), the Stoic.

Cato Censorius.basis: Burton applies Velleius's praise of the younger Cato to him
Cato Censorius.who: Marcus Porcius Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), Roman censor famous for his severity, who was prosecuted many times and always acquitted.

Catos.who: Cato used as a type: a severe, strait-laced moralist, after the Roman Catos.

Caucasus.who: The Caucasus, the mountain range between the Black and Caspian Seas, where Prometheus was chained.

Cauchinchina.who: Cochinchina, the southern part of present-day Vietnam, around the Mekong delta.

Caucut.who: Caldecote, a village near Nuneaton in north Warwickshire, seat of the Purefoy family.

Caussinus.who: Nicolas Caussin (1583–1651), French Jesuit, author of *De eloquentia sacra et humana* and confessor to Louis XIII.

Cavalerius.basis: he appears in a list of writers on Roman antiquities, and the Latin form fits
Cavalerius.who: Giovanni Battista de' Cavalieri (c. 1525–1601), Italian engraver who published plates of the antiquities and statues of Rome.

Cebes.who: Cebes of Thebes, a disciple of Socrates, to whom the *Tabula* (Pinax) is attributed, an allegorical picture of human life.

Celane.who: Celaene, one of the Proetides, the daughters of King Proetus who were driven mad and cured by the seer Melampus.

Celantia.who: Celantia, a Roman matron who received a letter of advice on Christian living, printed among Jerome's letters but now usually given to Pelagius.

Celestina.who: Celestina, the old bawd of Fernando de Rojas's Spanish tragicomedy *La Celestina* (1499), translated into Latin by Caspar Barth as *Pornoboscodidascalus*.

Celia.basis: the first passage is certain; the 'Celia in her Epistles' of the second is a different, unidentified source
Celia.who: In the first passage, Celia, the virtuous wife whom Volpone tries to seduce in Ben Jonson's comedy *Volpone, or the Fox* (1606).

Celts.who: The Celts, the ancient peoples of Gaul and central Europe.

Cenchreae.who: Cenchreae, the eastern port of ancient Corinth on the Saronic Gulf.

Censor Fulvius.who: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, Roman censor in 174 BC, who stripped marble tiles from Juno Lacinia's temple at Croton for his temple of Fortuna Equestris.

Censorinus.who: Censorinus, 3rd-century Roman grammarian, author of *De die natali* (238), addressed to Quintus Caerellius.

Censorius.basis: Plutarch's Crassus names Censorinus among those who died with Publius; Burton's form is garbled
Censorius.who: Censorinus, a young Roman nobleman and friend of Publius Crassus who died with him at Carrhae in 53 BC.

Centaur.who: Chiron the Centaur, the wise half-horse of Greek myth who taught healing and music.

Centaurs.who: The Centaurs, mythical half-man, half-horse creatures, famous for their drunken fight with the Lapiths.

Cephalus.who: Cephalus, mythical Athenian hero loved by Aurora; he was the husband of Procris and is said to have leapt from the Leucadian rock.

Cerberus.who: Cerberus, the many-headed dog that guarded the entrance to Hades in Greek myth.

Ceres.who: Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain and agriculture.

Cerinthus.who: Cerinthus, the lover of the poet Sulpicia in the elegies of the Tibullan collection.

Cermisonum.who: Antonio Cermisone (d. 1441), Italian physician who taught at Padua and Pavia, author of medical *Consilia*.

Cerotes.who: Cerates: stiff medicinal ointments made with wax.

Cesario Trento.basis: The Trento villas at Costozza were known for their cave ventilation, but I cannot confirm this particular Trento.
Cesario Trento.who: A member of the Trento family of Vicenza, whose villa at Costozza was famous for cooling air piped in from nearby caves.

Cestius Gallus.who: Gaius Cestius Gallus, Roman senator under Tiberius, known for his debauchery and extravagance.

Chaerea.who: Chaerea, the lovestruck young man in Terence's comedy *Eunuchus*.

Chaeronaea.who: Chaeronea in Boeotia, where Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes in 338 BC.

Chalcedony.who: Chalcedony, a kind of quartz used as a gemstone.

Chalcidius.who: Calcidius (4th century AD), Latin translator of and commentator on Plato's *Timaeus*.

Chalcocondila.who: Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1430–c. 1470), Byzantine Greek historian of the rise of the Ottomans, whose account of Britain includes this tale about wives.

Chaldaeorum.who: The Chaldeans, Babylonian astrologers and diviners.

Chaldean.who: The Chaldeans, the priestly caste of Babylon.

Chaldean Astrologers.who: The Chaldeans, the astrologers of ancient Babylon.

Chaldean Mithrobarzanes.who: Mithrobarzanes, the Chaldean magus and follower of Zoroaster who leads Menippus down to Hades in Lucian's *Menippus (Necyomantia)*.

Chaldeans.who: The Chaldeans, the people of ancient Babylonia, famous for their priests and astrologers.

Chaldees.who: The Chaldeans, the sages and astrologers of ancient Babylonia.

Chalderinian.basis: Montanus was a physician of Verona, and the form fits the Latin name for Caldiero.
Chalderinian.who: The thermal baths of Caldiero near Verona, in northern Italy.

Chaloner.who: Sir Thomas Chaloner the elder (1521–1565), English diplomat and author of the Latin poem *De republica Anglorum instauranda* in ten books.

Cham.who: The Great Khan, the title of the Mongol (Tartar) emperor.

Chamber.who: John Chamber (1546–1604), English cleric and author of *A Treatise against Judicial Astrologie* (1601).

Chamico.who: Chamico, a Peruvian narcotic plant related to datura (thorn-apple).

Chams.who: The Great Khans, rulers of the Mongols (Tartars).

Chamus.basis: Plutarch tells this story of a Carian; 'Chamus' seems to be a garbled name or ethnic in Burton's source.
Chamus.who: The Carian soldier in Plutarch's *Life of Artaxerxes* who claimed he had wounded Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa (401 BC), and boasted until he went mad.

Chaos.who: Chaos, meaning confusion or formless disorder.

Charassan.who: Khorasan, the region of north-eastern Iran and adjoining Central Asia that includes ancient Bactria.

Charenton.who: Charenton (now Charenton-le-Pont), a village just south-east of Paris, on the Marne.

Chariclea.who: Chariclea, the heroine of Heliodorus' Greek romance *Aethiopica* (Theagenes and Chariclea).

Charicles.who: Two fictional characters: in the first passage, a speaker in the Lucianic *Amores*; in the second, a lovesick youth in Aristaenetus' *Letters* (1.13).

Charidemus.who: Charidemus, the speaker and title of a dialogue on beauty attributed to Lucian (*Charidemus*).

Charity.who: Charity (Christian love), as a section heading.

Charles.who: In the first two passages Charlemagne (c. 742–814); in the third Emperor Charles V (1500–1558), who abdicated in favour of his son Philip II.

Charmides.who: Plato's dialogue *Charmides*, named after Charmides (d. 403 BC), Plato's uncle and a famously handsome youth; the second passage means the man himself.

Charon.who: Charon, ferryman of the dead, who tours the world with Hermes in Lucian's dialogue *Charon (Contemplantes)*.

Charybdis.who: Charybdis, the mythical whirlpool in the Strait of Messina, facing Scylla.

Chaucerum.who: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400), English poet, author of *Troilus and Criseyde*.

Chauci.who: The Chauci, a Germanic tribe on the North Sea coast between the Ems and the Elbe.

Checkley.who: Checkley, a village and parish in Staffordshire, England.

Chelidonium.basis: Burton cites Aristaenetus book 2, letter 13; she appears to be a character in that collection
Chelidonium.who: Chelidonion, a woman letter-writer in the fictional Love Letters of Aristaenetus (fl. c. 5th century AD).

Chelidonius.who: The chelidonius or swallow-stone, a stone said in the old lapidaries to be found in a swallow's belly.

Chersonesi.who: Chersonesi: Latin plural of 'chersonese', meaning peninsulas.

Cheshire.who: Cheshire, county in north-west England; the omen of floating tree-trunks was linked to the Brereton family.

Chica.basis: Burton speaks of Patagonian giants, and early maps place a region called Chica there
Chica.who: Chica, a region of southern South America shown on early maps, roughly Patagonia, where travellers reported giants.

Childericus.basis: More than one Merovingian Childeric fits: Childeric I was exiled by his subjects and Childeric II was murdered

Chile.who: Chile, Spanish colony on the Pacific coast of South America; Arica is now in northern Chile.

Chilo.basis: I cannot confirm who this addressee of Gregory Nazianzen was

Chilpericus.who: Chilperic I (c. 539–584), Merovingian king of Neustria, assassinated in 584; tradition blamed his queen Fredegund.

Chimeras.who: Chimeras: fantastic monsters or fancies, named after the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth.

Chiron.who: Chiron, the wise centaur of Greek myth, skilled in healing and music, who taught Achilles and Asclepius.

Chloe.who: Chloe, the heroine of Longus's Greek pastoral romance Daphnis and Chloe (2nd–3rd century AD).

Chloris.who: Chloris, a stock pastoral name for a shepherdess or mistress, used here in a lover's list of passing loves.

Choa.basis: Strabo and Valerius Maximus record this custom for Ceos, and Choa looks like a variant of its name
Choa.who: Ceos (modern Kea), Aegean island in the Cyclades, where ancient writers say the old took hemlock rather than outlive their strength.

Choaspis.who: The Choaspes, river of ancient Persia flowing past Susa (modern Karkheh, south-west Iran); the Persian kings drank only its water.

Choler.who: Choler: yellow bile, one of the four humours, hot and dry.

Choleric.who: Choleric: of or relating to choler (yellow bile).

Chorus Sancti Viti.who: Chorus Sancti Viti: St Vitus's dance, the dancing mania or chorea.

Chremes.who: Chremes, the meddling old neighbour of Menedemus in Terence's comedy Heauton Timorumenos (The Self-Tormentor, 163 BC).

Chremylus.who: Chremylus, the poor Athenian farmer who is the main character of Aristophanes' comedy Plutus (388 BC).

Christ.who: Jesus Christ; in the first passage the word is part of 'Christ Church', the Oxford college.

Christ Church.who: Christ Church, Oxford, the college refounded by Henry VIII in 1546, where Burton was a student from 1599 until his death.

Christ Church Oxon.who: Christ Church, Oxford, Burton's own college.

Christian.who: Christian (adjective); the prince meant is not named.

Christiani Crassiani.who: A Latin pun: 'Christians are Crassians', that is, dull or gross (from crassus, thick).

Christina.basis: A queen in a Polish chronicle anecdote about Władysław; I cannot confirm her identity, and the queen of Władysław II was named Agnes

Christoph. Ayrerus.basis: The medical-consultation context and the Latinised name fit; I am not sure of his dates
Christoph. Ayrerus.who: Christoph Ayrer, German physician of the late 16th century whose medical consultations were printed in collections of consilia.

Christoph. Columbus.who: Christopher Columbus (1451–1506), Genoese navigator who reached America in 1492.

Christopher.who: St Christopher, legendary martyr and patron of travellers, a cult figure of the Golden Legend.

Christopher Fonseca.who: Cristóbal de Fonseca (c. 1550–1621), Spanish Augustinian writer whose treatise on the love of God was translated into Latin as Amphitheatrum amoris.

Christopher Rotman.who: Christoph Rothmann (d. c. 1600), astronomer to Landgrave William IV of Hesse-Kassel, whose letters with Tycho Brahe were published in the Epistolae astronomicae.

Christopher Scheiner.who: Christoph Scheiner (1573/75–1650), German Jesuit astronomer who observed sunspots and wrote Rosa Ursina (1626–30).

Christopher Urswick.who: Christopher Urswick (1448–1522), English priest and diplomat, almoner to Henry VII, who declined the bishopric of Norwich.

Christophorus Ayrerus.basis: Cited alongside Hildesheim's Spicilegium, which collects consilia of German physicians; dates and works uncertain.
Christophorus Ayrerus.who: Christoph Ayrer, German physician whose medical opinions are quoted in Hildesheim's Spicilegia.

Christophorus à Vega.who: Cristóbal de Vega (1510–1573), Spanish physician and professor at Alcalá, physician to Philip II, author of medical commentaries and case-books.

Christs.who: Impostors who claimed to be Christ (false messiahs).

Chrysalus.who: Chrysalus, a fictional Persian prince in Celio Calcagnini's fable, turned by Jupiter into a butterfly.

Chrysippus.who: Chrysippus of Soli (c. 279–c. 206 BC), third head of the Stoic school at Athens and its chief systematiser.

Chrysis.who: Chrysis, a courtesan advised by the older Ampelis in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Chrysologus.who: St Peter Chrysologus (c. 380–c. 450), bishop of Ravenna, famed for his sermons.

Chunegunda.who: St Cunigunde of Luxembourg (c. 975–1040), wife of Emperor Henry II, said to have cleared herself of adultery by walking on red-hot ploughshares.

Cilia.who: Cilli, modern Celje in Slovenia, seat of the Counts of Cilli; Udalricus is Ulrich II of Cilli (1406–1456).

Cimmerian.who: The Cimmerians, a people placed by Homer at the edge of the world in perpetual darkness; hence 'Cimmerian darkness'.

Cincinnatus.who: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus (fl. 5th century BC), Roman statesman called from his plough to be dictator, then returned to his farm.

Cineas.who: Cineas (fl. c. 280 BC), Thessalian orator and adviser to King Pyrrhus of Epirus.

Cinyras.who: Cinyras, mythical king of Cyprus, tricked into incest by his daughter Myrrha, mother of Adonis.

Circassia.who: Circassia, region of the north-west Caucasus along the Black Sea coast.

Circe.who: Circe, the enchantress of the Odyssey who turned men into swine.

Circumcellions.who: The Circumcellions, fanatical bands of Donatists in 4th–5th-century North Africa, notorious for violence and seeking martyrdom.

Cirknickzerksey.who: Lake Cerknica (Cerkniško jezero), an intermittent karst lake in Slovenia (former Carniola) that fills and drains periodically.

Cis.who: Cis (Cicely), the rustic sweetheart addressed in a burlesque love-poem.

Civitas Philippi.who: Philippi, ancient city in eastern Macedonia, northern Greece, with a Roman-era theatre.

Claramontius.who: Scipione Chiaramonti (1565–1652), Italian philosopher of Cesena, whose Antitycho (1621) defended Aristotelian cosmology against Tycho Brahe.

Clarence.who: Clarence, English ducal title (from Clare, Suffolk), here held by Lionel of Antwerp (1338–1368), son of Edward III.

Claude Abbeville.who: Claude d'Abbeville (d. 1632), French Capuchin missionary to Maranhão in Brazil, author of a history of the 1612–14 mission (1614).

Claudia Valesia.who: Claude of Valois (1547–1575), daughter (not sister) of Henry II of France and wife of Charles III, Duke of Lorraine.

Claudio.basis: Named with Nero in a list of notorious imperial lusts drawn from Suetonius.

Claudius.who: Mostly the Roman emperor Claudius (10 BC–AD 54); in 'Appius Claudius' the decemvir Appius Claudius Crassus (fl. 451–449 BC).

Claudius Abbeville.who: Claude d'Abbeville (d. 1632), French Capuchin missionary to Maranhão in Brazil, author of a history of the 1612–14 mission (1614).

Claudius Caesar.who: Claudius (10 BC–AD 54), Roman emperor from AD 41, whose fearfulness Suetonius describes.

Claudius Minoes.who: Claude Mignault (Minos) (c. 1536–1606), French humanist and jurist, best known for his commentary on Alciato's Emblemata.

Clavius.who: Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), German Jesuit mathematician and astronomer at Rome, who wrote commentaries on Sacrobosco's Sphere and on Euclid.

Clazomenian Hermotimus.who: Hermotimus of Clazomenae, early Greek philosopher, said to leave his body in trance while his soul wandered abroad.

Cleanthes.who: Cleanthes of Assos (c. 330–c. 230 BC), Stoic philosopher who succeeded Zeno; he was poor and did manual work at night, drawing water and grinding meal.

Clearchus.who: Clearchus, a fictional letter-writer in the Love Letters of Aristaenetus (c. 5th century AD).

Cleinias.who: Cleinias of Tarentum (4th century BC), Pythagorean philosopher who was said to calm his anger by playing the lyre.

Clemens.who: Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215), Greek Christian theologian, author of the Stromata (Miscellanies).

Clemens Alexandrinus.who: Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215), Greek Christian theologian, author of the Stromata (Miscellanies).

Clenard.who: Nicolas Cleynaerts (Clenardus) (c. 1495–1542), Flemish grammarian and traveller in Portugal, Spain and Morocco, whose Latin Letters were published.

Cleobulus.who: Cleobulus of Lindos (6th century BC), one of the Seven Sages of Greece; maxims about how to treat a wife are ascribed to him.

Cleodemus.who: Cleodemus, a Peripatetic philosopher in Lucian's dialogue Philopseudes (The Lover of Lies), who tells the story of the Hyperborean magician.

Cleombrotus Ambraciotes.who: Cleombrotus of Ambracia, Greek said to have thrown himself from a wall after reading Plato's Phaedo on the immortality of the soul.

Cleonymus.basis: The setting (a feast at the Piraeus, guests stunned by beauty) matches Aristaenetus, whom Burton cites nearby; not checked.
Cleonymus.who: Cleonymus, a beautiful youth in one of the fictional Love Letters of Aristaenetus.

Cleopatra.basis: The first passage names a gynaecological writer; the others the queen.
Cleopatra.who: Mostly Cleopatra VII (69–30 BC), queen of Egypt; in the medical passage, the 'Cleopatra' credited with an ancient treatise on women's diseases.

Cleves.who: Cleves (Kleve), a duchy on the lower Rhine; its mentally ill duke was Johann Wilhelm of Jülich-Cleves-Berg (1562–1609).

Clitipho.who: Clitipho, son of Chremes in Terence's comedy Heauton Timorumenos (The Self-Tormentor).

Clitophon.who: Clitophon, narrator and hero of Achilles Tatius's Greek romance Leucippe and Clitophon (2nd century AD).

Clitorius.who: The spring at Cleitor in Arcadia, whose water was said to give a distaste for wine; there Melampus was said to cure the daughters of Proetus.

Clitus.who: Cleitus the Black, Macedonian officer and friend of Alexander the Great, killed by Alexander in a drunken quarrel in 328 BC.

Cloacina.who: Cloacina, Roman goddess of the Cloaca Maxima, Rome's great sewer, later identified with Venus.

Clodoveus.basis: The first passage fits Clovis II exactly; the fair-haired king praised by Paulus Aemilius may be a different Clovis, probably Clovis I.
Clodoveus.who: In the first passage, Clovis II (d. c. 657), Frankish king and son of Dagobert I, said to have gone mad after violating the relics of St Denis.

Clytemnestra.who: Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon in Greek legend, who took Aegisthus as her lover and murdered her husband.

Cn. Pompeius.who: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, Pompey the Great (106–48 BC), Roman general and statesman.

Cobali.who: Kobolds, the goblins or spirits of the German mines, as Georgius Agricola describes them.

Cocytus.who: Cocytus, the river of wailing in the Greek underworld.

Codronchus.who: Giovanni Battista Codronchi (1547–1628), physician of Imola, who wrote on hydrophobia, on salt of wormwood and on hellebore.

Codrus.who: Codrus, legendary last king of Athens, who gave up his life to save the city from Dorian invaders.

Coele-Syria.who: Coele-Syria ('Hollow Syria'), the ancient name for southern Syria, centred on the Beqaa valley between the Lebanon ranges, often extended to Damascus.

Cogitation.who: A faculty of the mind in Renaissance psychology.

Cogitative.who: A term of faculty psychology for the imagination or inner sense.

Coimbra.who: Coimbra in Portugal; Burton means the Conimbricenses, the Jesuits of its university, whose commentaries on Aristotle were published 1592–1606.

Colerus.basis: The cited title De immortalitate animae fits Coler's work; his dates are not certain.
Colerus.who: Jacob Coler (Colerus), German Lutheran theologian, author of a treatise on the immortality of the soul.

Collalto.basis: This is the best-known Collalto with a commanding prospect, but other places in Italy have the name.
Collalto.who: Collalto, a hill-top castle and village near Treviso in the Veneto, seat of the counts of Collalto.

Collatine.who: Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, Lucretia's husband in Roman legend, whose praise of her inflamed Sextus Tarquinius.

Collatinus.who: Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, husband of Lucretia in Roman legend, and one of the first consuls of Rome.

Colliget.who: The Colliget (Kitab al-Kulliyyat), the medical encyclopedia of Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), much used in Latin translation.

Collignius.basis: An authority on the French civil wars; Gaspard de Coligny (d. 1572) doesn't fit securely.

Cologne.who: Cologne (Köln), city on the Rhine in Germany, seat of an archbishopric and said to hold the relics of the Three Kings.

Colon.who: The colon, part of the large intestine.

Colophon.who: Colophon, ancient Ionian Greek city near modern Izmir, Turkey, whose territory held the oracle of Apollo at Claros.

Colossus.who: The Colossus of Rhodes, giant bronze statue of Helios, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

Columbina.who: Colombina, a conventional mistress's name, as in the serving-maid of Italian commedia dell'arte.

Columbus.basis: The anatomist is the one cited alongside Vesalius and Crooke.
Columbus.who: In the anatomy passage, Realdo Colombo (c. 1516–1559), Italian anatomist; elsewhere Christopher Columbus (1451–1506), Genoese navigator who reached America.

Columni.who: The Colonna, a powerful Roman baronial family, enemies of Pope Alexander VI (Borgia).

Colures.who: Colures, the two great circles of the celestial sphere passing through the poles and the equinoxes or solstices.

Combabus.who: Combabus, legendary courtier in Lucian's *On the Syrian Goddess* who castrated himself before escorting Queen Stratonice, to escape suspicion.

Commodus.who: Commodus (161–192), Roman emperor 180–192, notorious for his excesses.

Common Sense.who: The 'common sense', in faculty psychology the inward sense that unites the reports of the outward senses.

Complutum.who: Complutum, the Roman name of Alcalá de Henares, near Madrid, Spain.

Composition.basis: Scholastic term for an act of the understanding.

Compostella.who: Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, Spain, the great pilgrimage shrine of St James.

Comus.who: Comus, Greco-Roman god of revelry, feasting and nocturnal merrymaking.

Conciliator.who: Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–c. 1316), Italian physician and philosopher, called 'the Conciliator' after his *Conciliator differentiarum*.

Conclave Ignatii.who: *Conclave Ignati* (1611), John Donne's satire on the Jesuits, translated into English as *Ignatius his Conclave*.

Confess.who: St Augustine's *Confessions*, where he recalls weeping over Dido.

Congo.who: The Kingdom of Kongo, in west-central Africa around the lower Congo river.

Conimbricenses.who: The Conimbricenses, Jesuits of the University of Coimbra in Portugal who published a famous series of commentaries on Aristotle (1592–1606).

Conqueror.who: William the Conqueror (c. 1028–1087), Duke of Normandy and King of England from 1066, son of Duke Robert and Arlette.

Conradinus.who: Conradin (1252–1268), last Hohenstaufen Duke of Swabia, beheaded at Naples by Charles of Anjou.

Conradus.basis: Matthew Paris tells a similar astrologer story of Frederick II, so it is unclear which emperor is meant.

Conradus Gesner.who: Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), Zurich physician and naturalist, author of the *Historia animalium*.

Constantine.who: Mostly Constantine the Great (c. 272–337), Roman emperor who fought Licinius; the agriculture citation is to the Byzantine *Geoponica*, compiled under Constantine VII.

Constantine Despota.basis: A Byzantine despot named by Nicephorus Gregoras; I can't identify him with confidence.

Constantinople.who: Constantinople, modern Istanbul, the Ottoman capital.

Constantinopoli.who: Constantinople (modern Istanbul); a Latin form meaning 'at Constantinople'.

Constantinus.basis: 'Const. lib. de agric.' is the usual early-modern way of citing the Geoponica.
Constantinus.who: The *Geoponica*, Byzantine farming compilation made under Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (905–959), cited under his name.

Constantinus Africanus.who: Constantinus Africanus (d. c.1087), North African monk of Monte Cassino who translated Arabic medical works into Latin, including a treatise on melancholy.

Constantius.who: Constantius II (317–361), Roman emperor from 337 who favoured the Arian party in the Church.

Contarenus.who: Gasparo Contarini (1483–1542), Venetian statesman and cardinal, author of *De magistratibus et republica Venetorum*, on the Venetian constitution.

Contempt.who: A personified abstraction in a list of the prodigal's companions, not a proper name.

Contempts.who: An ordinary word in a section heading.

Contention.who: An ordinary word: the vice opposite to flattery.

Contiles.who: Luca Contile (1505–1574), Italian man of letters, author of a treatise on imprese (emblematic devices) published in 1574.

Contumelies.who: An ordinary word in a section heading.

Contumely.who: Contumely (insolence) personified as a deity; Cicero mentions shrines to Contumely and Impudence at Athens.

Convulsion.who: A disease of the nerves, not a proper name.

Copernicus.who: Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), Polish astronomer who proposed the heliocentric system.

Coppinger.who: Edmund Coppinger (d. 1592), fanatical follower of William Hacket; with Henry Arthington he proclaimed Hacket the Messiah in London in 1591.

Coptus.who: Coptos, ancient town in Upper Egypt on the Nile, modern Qift.

Coquage.who: Cocuage, Rabelais's mock god of cuckolds in the *Tiers Livre* of *Pantagruel*.

Corcutus.who: Şehzade Korkut (c.1467–1513), scholarly son of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II, passed over for the throne and put to death by his brother Selim I.

Corcyra.who: Corcyra, the Ionian island of Corfu (Kerkyra), off north-western Greece, which was traditionally identified with the Phaeacians' land.

Corderoy.basis: The context is English writers against atheism, and Corderoy's book of that kind fits.
Corderoy.who: Jeremy Corderoy, early 17th-century Oxford divine, author of *A Warning for Worldlings* (1608), a dialogue against atheists.

Cordus.who: Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), German botanist and pharmacist whose *Dispensatorium* became the official pharmacopoeia of Nuremberg.

Corelia.who: Karelia, a region between the Gulf of Finland and the White Sea, now divided between Finland and Russia.

Corellius Rufus.who: Quintus Corellius Rufus (d. c.98 AD), Roman consular and friend of Pliny the Younger, who starved himself to death to escape the pain of gout.

Coresus.who: Coresus, legendary priest of Dionysus at Calydon who loved Callirhoe in vain and killed himself in her place when she was to be sacrificed (Pausanias 7.21).

Corinna.basis: Burton seems to put a stock name for a beloved into his English rendering of the kissing verses; Ovid's Corinna is the usual source.
Corinna.who: Corinna, the mistress celebrated in Ovid's *Amores*, used here as a conventional name for a poet's beloved.

Corinthians.who: The Christians of Corinth to whom Paul wrote his Corinthian epistles.

Coriolanus.who: Gnaeus Marcius Coriolanus, legendary Roman general of the 5th century BC; he was exiled, led the Volscians against Rome, and his mother and wife persuaded him to withdraw.

Cornelia.who: Cornelia (2nd century BC), daughter of Scipio Africanus and mother of the Gracchi, a model of Roman matronly virtue.

Cornelius.basis: The centurion is certain from the theological context; the friar is identified from Meteren's history and the epithet 'of Dort'.
Cornelius.who: In the later passages, Cornelius the centurion, a Gentile accepted by God (Acts 10); in the first, Friar Cornelis Adriaensen of Dordrecht (1521–1581), Franciscan preacher at Bruges.

Cornelius Agrippa.who: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535), German physician and occultist, author of *De occulta philosophia*.

Cornelius Drebbel.who: Cornelis Drebbel (1572–1633), Dutch inventor at the court of James I, famous for his perpetual-motion device; he wrote a treatise on the nature of the elements.

Cornelius Gallus.who: Gaius Cornelius Gallus (c.70–26 BC), Roman elegiac poet; the verses Burton quotes come from Maximianus's elegies, which were then ascribed to Gallus.

Cornelius Gemma.who: Cornelius Gemma (1535–1578), physician and astronomer at Louvain, author of the *Cosmocritice* on prodigies and celestial influences.

Cornelius Mussus.who: Cornelio Musso (1511–1574), Franciscan preacher celebrated across Italy, later Bishop of Bitonto.

Cornelius Nepos.who: Cornelius Nepos (c.110–c.24 BC), Roman biographer whose surviving works include the life of his friend Atticus.

Cornelius Rufus.who: Burton's slip for Quintus Corellius Rufus (d. c.98 AD), Pliny the Younger's friend, whose death Pliny mourns in his letter to Calestrius Tiro (Ep. 1.12).

Cornelius Tacitus.who: Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c.56–c.120), Roman historian, author of the *Annals*; in the second passage Burton puns on *tacitus* ('silent') against *cornutus* ('horned').

Cornuto.who: Italian for a cuckold ('horned one'), not a proper name.

Cornwall.who: Cornwall, county in south-west England, the subject of Richard Carew's *Survey of Cornwall* (1602).

Coroebus.who: Coroebus, Phrygian son of Mygdon who came to Troy for love of Cassandra and was killed when the city fell (Virgil, *Aeneid* 2).

Cortesius.who: Martín Cortés de Albacar (1510–1582), Spanish cosmographer whose *Breve compendio de la sphera y de la arte de navegar* (1551) discussed the compass's variation.

Corvini.who: Men like Marcus Valerius Corvus, Roman hero who, aided by a raven, killed a Gallic champion in single combat in 349 BC (Livy 7).

Corvus.basis: Named among chiromancers alongside Johannes de Indagine and Tricasso, which fits Corvo's palmistry manual.
Corvus.who: Andrea Corvo of Mirandola, Italian chiromancer of the early sixteenth century, whose handbook on palmistry was widely reprinted.

Corybantes.who: The Corybantes, frenzied priests of the Phrygian mother-goddess Cybele, who worshipped her with wild armed dances and drumming.

Corybantiasmi.who: Burton's coinage from the Greek for 'Corybantic frenzy', after Cybele's raving priests; here, frantic would-be poets.

Corydon’s Phyllis.who: Corydon and Phyllis, a stock shepherd and shepherdess of pastoral poetry, taken from Virgil's Eclogues.

Cosmo Paccio Interpret.basis: Burton's marginal note names the translator of Maximus Tyrius.
Cosmo Paccio Interpret.who: Cosimo de' Pazzi, archbishop of Florence, who made the Latin translation of the dissertations of Maximus of Tyre (published 1517).

Cosmography.who: Cosmography: the description of the world, i.e. geography.

Cosmus.who: Mostly Cosimo de' Medici the Elder (1389–1464), banker and ruler of Florence; in the second passage, Saint Cosmas, physician-martyr always paired with his brother Damian.

Cosmus Medices.who: In the first two passages, Cosimo de' Medici the Elder (1389–1464), ruler of Florence; in the third, Cosimo I de' Medici (1519–1574), Duke of Florence and Jovius's patron.

Coster.who: Franciscus Costerus (Frans de Costere, 1532–1619), Flemish Jesuit controversialist, author of an Enchiridion of controversies defending Catholic doctrine.

Costoza.who: Costozza, near Longare outside Vicenza, famous for villas cooled by air drawn from natural caves through underground ducts.

Cotswold.who: The Cotswolds, the upland sheep country of Gloucestershire, famous for fine wool.

Cotta.who: First passage: John Cotta (c.1575–1650), Northampton physician who wrote against ignorant practitioners. Otherwise: Gaius Aurelius Cotta, Roman consul 75 BC, orator in Sallust and Academic speaker in Cicero's De natura deorum.

Cotys.who: Cotys I, king of the Odrysian Thracians (r. c.384–360 BC); Plutarch tells the anecdote about him breaking the gift of glassware.

Coubert.who: Coubert, a village in Brie (Seine-et-Marne) south-east of Paris, seat of the lords of Vitry.

Courtier.who: Il Cortegiano (The Book of the Courtier, 1528) by Baldassare Castiglione, the classic portrait of the ideal courtier.

Coveting.who: Translation of 'concupiscible', the desiring power of the soul in scholastic psychology.

Cracovia.who: Kraków, then the royal capital and university city of Poland.

Crales.who: Stefan Uroš II Milutin (r. 1282–1321), king of Serbia ('Crales' renders kral, 'king'), who sought to marry Eudokia, sister of Emperor Andronikos II.

Crantor.who: Crantor of Soli (c.335–c.275 BC), Academic philosopher whose treatise On Grief was the model for ancient consolations.

Cranzius.who: Albert Krantz (c.1450–1517), Hamburg historian, author of chronicles of Saxony, the Wends and Scandinavia.

Crassus.who: First passage: Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus (consul 131 BC), lawyer and pontifex maximus. Otherwise: Marcus Licinius Crassus (d. 53 BC), the triumvir proverbial for his wealth.

Crates.who: Crates of Thebes (c.365–c.285 BC), Cynic philosopher who gave away his wealth and was revered at Athens as a peacemaker.

Crates Thebanus.who: Crates of Thebes (c.365–c.285 BC), Cynic philosopher who gave away his fortune to live in voluntary poverty.

Cratevas.who: Crateuas, Greek herbalist addressed in a spurious letter of Hippocrates; the name is that of the famous root-cutter of Mithridates VI.

Cratisthenes.who: Cratisthenes, the hero's friend in Eustathius Macrembolites' twelfth-century Byzantine romance Hysmine and Hysminias.

Crecy.who: Crécy-en-Ponthieu in Picardy, scene of Edward III's victory over the French in 1346.

Creed.who: The Apostles' Creed; in the first passage it is part of the title of Thomas Jackson's Commentaries upon the Creed.

Crellius.who: Johann Crell (1590–1633), German-born Socinian theologian who taught at the Racovian academy in Poland.

Crema.who: Crema, a walled town in Lombardy between Milan and Cremona, then under Venice.

Cremona.who: Cremona, a city on the Po in Lombardy.

Creseida.basis: The Petronius passage (Satyricon 130) has Encolpius feeding on onions and snails for Circe; Burton seems to substitute a generic lover's name.
Creseida.who: Cressida, Troilus's faithless love, used here as a stock name for a mistress; in Petronius the lover is Encolpius, preparing himself for Circe.

Cresence.who: Cardinal Marcello Crescenzi (1500–1552), papal legate presiding at the Council of Trent, who died at Verona.

Cressetlight.who: A comic made-up name in a burlesque rustic love-letter (a cresset is an iron fire-basket used as a lamp).

Cressida.who: Cressida, the Trojan woman who deserted Troilus for Diomedes in medieval and Shakespearean story.

Crete.who: Crete, the large Greek island in the eastern Mediterranean.

Criseyde.who: Criseyde, heroine of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.

Crisis.basis: Spelling of 'crasis', the bodily temperament or constitution.

Crispin.who: St Crispin (d. c. 286), Roman martyr in Gaul, patron saint of shoemakers.

Critias.basis: The first passage cites Plato's dialogue; the others mean the man.
Critias.who: Critias (c. 460–403 BC), Athenian associate of Socrates and leader of the Thirty Tyrants; also the title of a dialogue by Plato named after him (first passage).

Crito.who: Crito of Alopece, wealthy Athenian friend of Socrates, who appears in Plato's Crito and Phaedo.

Critobulus.who: Critobulus, son of Crito, young Athenian companion of Socrates; he speaks in Xenophon's Oeconomicus and Symposium.

Croatia.who: Croatia, a Balkan country on the Adriatic.

Crobyle.who: Crobyle, a character in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans; she is a mother training her daughter Corinna as a courtesan.

Croesi.basis: A Latin plural: 'men as rich as Croesus'.
Croesi.who: Croesus (r. c. 560–546 BC), king of Lydia, proverbial for his wealth.

Croesus.who: Croesus (r. c. 560–546 BC), king of Lydia, proverbial for his wealth, visited by Solon in Herodotus' account.

Crollius.who: Oswald Croll (c. 1560–1609), German Paracelsian physician and chemist, author of the Basilica chymica (1609).

Cromatius.who: Chromatius (d. c. 407), bishop of Aquileia and friend and correspondent of Jerome.

Cromerus.who: Marcin Kromer (1512–1589), Polish historian and prince-bishop of Warmia, author of De origine et rebus gestis Polonorum.

Cromwell.who: Thomas Cromwell (c. 1485–1540), minister of Henry VIII; Foxe tells how he later repaid his early help from the Florentine merchant Frescobaldi.

Croton.who: Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy (modern Crotone); in Petronius' Satyricon it is a town full of legacy-hunters.

Crotonienses.who: The people of Croton in southern Italy; a smaller army from Locri defeated them at the river Sagra in the 6th century BC.

Crowland.who: Crowland in the Lincolnshire fens, where St Guthlac (d. 714) lived as a hermit and where Crowland Abbey was later founded.

Ctesias.who: Ctesias of Cnidus (fl. c. 400 BC), Greek physician at the Persian court, author of the Persica and Indica.

Cucubuth.basis: Arabic medical term used by Avicenna for lycanthropy.

Cuddesdon.who: Cuddesdon, a village near Oxford, site of the palace of the bishops of Oxford built by Bishop John Bancroft.

Culmannus.basis: He is the best-known writer of this Latin name who fits a list of Protestant consolatory authors.
Culmannus.who: Leonhard Culmann (16th century), German Lutheran pastor and writer of devotional and educational works.

Cuman.who: Cumae, an ancient Greek colony near Naples; the ass of Cumae that wore a lion's skin was proverbial for an impostor.

Cumberland.who: Cumberland (Cumbria), in north-west England, once held by Scottish kings; 'Prince of Cumberland' was a title of the heir to the Scottish throne.

Cumea.basis: The form and the Apollo context suggest Cumae; Cyme in Aeolis is a possible alternative.
Cumea.who: Cumae, an ancient Greek city in Campania near Naples, home of Apollo's Sibyl.

Cupid.who: Cupid, the Roman god of love, son of Venus.

Cupids.who: Cupid, the Roman god of love; Cicero's De natura deorum separates three gods of this name.

Cupid’s Statue.who: Cupid, the Roman god of love; here a statue of him.

Curii.who: Manius Curius Dentatus (d. 270 BC), Roman consul and general, an exemplar of old Roman frugality; 'Curii' means men like him.

Curio.who: First passage: Johannes Curio, 16th-century German physician who commented on the Schola Salernitana; second: Gaius Scribonius Curio the elder (consul 76 BC), who attacked Caesar's morals.

Curiosity.basis: Ordinary word used as a heading.

Curius.who: Manius Curius Dentatus (d. 270 BC), Roman consul who defeated Pyrrhus, proverbial for frugality and incorruptibility.

Curtii.who: Marcus Curtius, legendary Roman youth who rode into a chasm in the Forum to save the city; 'Curtii' means men like him.

Cusanus.who: Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), German cardinal, philosopher and mathematician who speculated on an unbounded universe.

Cusco.basis: Las Casas was actually bishop of Chiapas, so the attribution is Burton's error.
Cusco.who: Cuzco (Cusco), the former Inca capital in Peru.

Cuspinian.who: Johannes Cuspinian (1473–1529), Viennese humanist, diplomat and historian, author of De Caesaribus atque imperatoribus Romanis.

Cuzco.who: Cuzco, the old Inca capital in the Andes of southern Peru, whose temples Acosta described.

Cyanean.basis: The Euxine passages mean the Symplegades; the Lycian one means Cyaneae (Pausanias 7).
Cyanean.who: Usually the Cyanean Rocks or Symplegades, the 'clashing' islets at the Black Sea mouth of the Bosporus; in the Lycian passage, Cyaneae, a Lycian town with an oracle of Apollo Thyrxeus.

Cyclopes.who: The Cyclopes, the one-eyed giants of Greek myth, here run together with the Giants who warred on the gods.

Cyclops.who: Polyphemus the Cyclops as shown in Euripides' satyr play *Cyclops*, where he boasts that he worships only his belly.

Cyclops Polyphemus.who: Polyphemus, the one-eyed giant of Greek myth who loved the sea-nymph Galatea in vain (Theocritus, Ovid).

Cydippe.who: Cydippe, the maiden in Greek legend whom Acontius won by tricking her into an oath on an inscribed apple (Callimachus; Ovid, *Heroides* 20–21).

Cygno.who: The constellation Cygnus (the Swan), where a new star, now called P Cygni, appeared in 1600.
