Cymon.who: Cimone, the boorish youth of Cyprus whom love for Efigenia makes civilised, in Boccaccio's *Decameron* (5.1).

Cynics.who: The Cynics, the Greek philosophical sect of Antisthenes and Diogenes, who scorned wealth, convention and honours.

Cyniras.who: Cinyras, legendary king of Cyprus, whose daughter Myrrha loved him incestuously and bore Adonis (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 10).

Cynocephalus.who: Anubis, the dog-headed Egyptian god who in the myth helped Isis in her mourning search for Osiris.

Cynops.who: Cynops, a sorcerer of Patmos who contends with St John in the apocryphal Acts of John ascribed to Prochorus.

Cynosure.who: Cynosura, the Little Bear and its pole star, by which sailors steered; so, a guiding star.

Cynthia.who: In Martial's line, Cynthia, the mistress celebrated in Propertius' elegies; elsewhere simply a poetic or Italian girl's name.

Cyparissae.basis: The citation of Constantine's agriculture book 10 (the *Geoponica*, on trees) fits the cypress myth.
Cyparissae.who: The daughters of Eteocles (in legend, king of Orchomenus) who were turned into cypress trees, as told in the Byzantine *Geoponica*.

Cyprian Eichovius.who: Cyprianus Eichovius, German compiler of the *Deliciae Hispaniae* (Cologne, 1604), a collection of descriptions of Spain.

Cyprus.who: Cyprus, the eastern Mediterranean island, in antiquity sacred to Venus.

Cyril.who: St Cyril of Alexandria (d. 444), patriarch and theologian, who wrote a refutation of the emperor Julian's attack on Christianity.

Cyropaed.who: Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*, an idealised account of the education and reign of Cyrus the Great.

Cyrus.who: In the Xenophon passages, Cyrus the Great (d. 530 BC), founder of the Persian empire; in Plutarch's *Artaxerxes*, Cyrus the Younger, killed at Cunaxa in 401 BC.

Cyzeni.who: The people of Cyzicus, a Greek city on the Sea of Marmara, where Pliny places a spring of Cupid that cures love.

Cyzicum.who: Cyzicus, Greek city on the Sea of Marmara (Kapıdağ peninsula, Turkey), unsuccessfully besieged by Mithridates VI in 73 BC.

Cyzicus.who: Cyzicus, an ancient Greek city on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara, now in ruins in Turkey.

D. Claudius.who: 'Divus Claudius', the emperor Claudius (r. AD 41–54), deified after his death.

D. Hadrianus.who: 'Divus Hadrianus', the emperor Hadrian (r. AD 117–138), deified after his death.

Daedalian.who: An adjective from Daedalus, the mythical master craftsman: so, intricately ingenious.

Daedalus.who: Daedalus, the legendary Athenian craftsman and sculptor, builder of the Cretan labyrinth.

Dagobert.who: Dagobert I (d. 639), Merovingian king of the Franks and patron of the abbey of Saint-Denis; father of Clovis II.

Dagon.who: Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines in the Old Testament (Judges 16; 1 Samuel 5).

Dalecampius.who: Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), French physician and botanist of Lyon, compiler of the *Historia generalis plantarum* (1586–87).

Dalliance.who: An allegorical figure, personified pleasure-making, in a symbolic picture of Opulentia (Wealth).

Damagetus.who: Damagetus, the addressee of the spurious Hippocratic letters describing Hippocrates' visit to Democritus at Abdera.

Damascen.basis: The cited works separate three different Damasceni; the medical one is the least certain.
Damascen.who: In *De orthodoxa fide*, St John of Damascus (d. c. 750), Greek theologian; on the Celts, Nicolaus of Damascus; 'Damascen the Arabian' is the Arabic medical author Johannes Damascenus.

Damascus.who: Damascus, the ancient city of Syria, famous for its gardens and waters.

Damasippus.who: Damasippus, a bankrupt art-dealer turned Stoic who, in Horace's *Satires* 2.3, argues that all fools are mad.

Damian.who: St Damian, with his twin St Cosmas a physician martyred in Syria (c. 300), patron saint of physicians; the two are always paired.

Damianus à Goes.who: Damião de Góis (1502–1574), Portuguese humanist and chronicler, who wrote a Latin account of the Lapps.

Damiata.who: Damietta, a port on the eastern mouth of the Nile in the delta of Egypt.

Damon.who: Damon, the Pythagorean of Syracuse who offered his life as surety for his friend Pythias (Phintias) before the tyrant Dionysius.

Danae.who: Danaë, Argive princess whom Zeus visited as a shower of gold in her prison; she became the mother of Perseus.

Danaeus.who: Lambert Daneau (c.1530–1595), French Calvinist theologian who wrote a dialogue on witches, a treatise against games of chance, and a catalogue of heresies.

Danaus.basis: The first passage is clearly the mythical Danaus. The second probably is too: Pausanias tells of Danaus finding husbands for his daughters by a race, and 'Lacedaemon' looks like Burton's slip.
Danaus.who: Danaus, mythical king of Argos and son of Belus, father of the fifty Danaids.

Dandinus.who: Girolamo Dandini (1554–1634), Italian Jesuit philosopher, author of a commentary on Aristotle's De anima.

Dane.who: A native of Denmark; here describing the Danish physician Petrus Severinus.

Daniel Federer.basis: a patient known only from a case recorded by Schenck

Daniel Gare.basis: a subject of a horoscope in Camerarius; nothing further known

Daniel Sennertus.who: Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), German physician and professor of medicine at Wittenberg, author of a widely used medical textbook.

Dante.who: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy.

Dantes.who: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), Florentine poet whose Inferno describes hell.

Danubius.who: The Danube, the great river of central and south-eastern Europe.

Danvers.who: Henry Danvers, Earl of Danby (1573–1644), English soldier who founded the Oxford Physic Garden, now the Botanic Garden, in 1621.

Danzig.who: Danzig, now Gdańsk in Poland, a Baltic port in what was then Prussia ('Spruce').

Daphnaeus.who: Daphnaeus, a speaker in Plutarch's dialogue on love (Amatorius), where he praises marriage.

Daphne.who: Daphne, the nymph who fled from Apollo and was turned into a laurel (bay) tree.

Daphnis.basis: different figures: a girl in Aristaenetus' letters, a courtesan in Lucian's dialogues, and Theocritus' pastoral herdsman

Dares Phrygius.who: Dares Phrygius, the Trojan priest in Homer said to have written a history of Troy's fall; the surviving Latin prose version is late antique.

Darii.who: The Persian kings named Darius, used as a type of great wealth.

Darius.who: Darius III of Persia (r. 336–330 BC), defeated by Alexander, in the first two passages; Darius I (r. 522–486 BC) in the 1 Esdras story.

Darrell.who: John Darrell (b. c.1562), English Puritan exorcist whose claims to dispossess demoniacs set off a pamphlet war around 1599–1602.

Dasamonquepeuc.who: Dasamonquepeuc, an Algonquian village on the mainland facing Roanoke Island, North Carolina, described in the accounts of Raleigh's Virginia voyages.

Dathan.who: Dathan, an Israelite who rebelled with Korah against Moses and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16).

Daulis.who: Daulis, an ancient town in Phocis, central Greece, where the myth of Procne and Philomela was set (hence no swallows).

Dauphine.who: The Dauphiné, a former province of south-eastern France bordering Savoy.

David.who: David, king of Israel, traditionally the author of the Psalms.

David George.who: David Joris (c.1501–1556), Dutch glass-painter and Anabaptist leader from Delft, who claimed a messianic role.

David Helde.basis: a patient known only from Ruland's case

Dea Syria.who: The Syrian Goddess (Atargatis), whose inspiration Eunus claimed when he led the Sicilian slave revolt (c. 135 BC).

Deacon.who: John Deacon, co-author with John Walker of the Dialogicall Discourses of Spirits and Divels (1601) against Darrell; in the second passage 'the Deacon' is Philip the Evangelist.

Death.basis: common noun, personified in the Cupid fable

Deborah.who: Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, buried under the oak Allon Bachuth near Bethel (Genesis 35:8); not the judge Deborah.

Deccan.who: The Deccan, the plateau of south-central India, then ruled by several sultanates.

Decii.who: The Decii Mures, Roman consuls (father 340 BC, son 295 BC) who each devoted themselves to death in battle to win victory for Rome.

Decius.who: Decius (r. 249–251), Roman emperor who led the first empire-wide persecution of Christians.

Declamat.basis: abbreviation of 'Declamatio', a reference to a work by Beroaldus

Deianira.who: Deianira, wife of Hercules, who unknowingly killed him with the shirt poisoned with Nessus' blood.

Deidamia.who: Deidamia, daughter of King Lycomedes of Scyros, by whom Achilles, hidden there in women's clothes, fathered Pyrrhus (Neoptolemus).
